Deriving it from Taylor series: The same formula comes from the Taylor expansion you met in calculus: f(x0 + h) = f(x0) + h f'(x0) + (h^2 / 2) f''(x0) + ... We want f(x0 + h) = 0. If h is small, h^2 is tiny, so keep only the first two terms: f(x0) + h f'(x0) = 0, which gives h = -f(x0) / f'(x0). So Newton's method is "replace the curve by its straight-line Taylor approximation and solve that". The ignored h^2 term is the error, and it is also the reason for its speed, as we will see.

Worked example 1, square root of 2: f(x) = x^2 - 2, so f'(x) = 2x. The formula becomes x_new = x - (x^2 - 2) / (2x), which simplifies to x_new = (x + 2/x) / 2. That is exactly the Babylonian average rule. Start with x0 = 1. x1 = (1 + 2) / 2 = 1.5. x2 = (1.5 + 2/1.5) / 2 = (1.5 + 1.333333) / 2 = 1.4166667. x3 = 1.4142157. x4 = 1.4142135624. The true value is 1.41421356237.

Counting the correct digits: Look at the errors: 0.414, then 0.0858, then 0.00245, then 0.0000021, then 0.0000000000016. The number of correct digits goes roughly 0, 1, 2, 5, 11. Each error is about the square of the one before, times a constant. That is called quadratic convergence. The constant here is about 1/(2 times 1.414), roughly 0.35, so for example 0.35 times (0.00245)^2 is about 0.0000021.

Why quadratic: From the Taylor view, the error after a step is controlled by the h^2 term we threw away. Near a simple root r, the new error e_new is approximately (f''(r) / (2 f'(r))) times e_old^2. Square a small number and it becomes much smaller: 0.01 squared is 0.0001. That is why the digits double. But this only kicks in when you are already close; far from the root the h^2 term is not small and the guarantee disappears.

Worked example 2, Newton's own equation: f(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5, f'(x) = 3x^2 - 2. Start at x0 = 2. f(2) = -1 and f'(2) = 10, so x1 = 2 - (-1)/10 = 2.1. f(2.1) = 9.261 - 4.2 - 5 = 0.061, f'(2.1) = 3(4.41) - 2 = 11.23, so x2 = 2.1 - 0.061/11.23 = 2.0945681. One more step gives x3 = 2.0945515, correct to 7 decimal places. Compare: false position in the last lesson needed six steps to get only 3 or 4 correct decimals.

Worked example 3, division without dividing: Early computers and some processors find 1/a without a divide instruction. Take f(x) = 1/x - a. Then Newton gives x_new = x (2 - a x), only multiplication and subtraction. For a = 7 starting at x0 = 0.1: x1 = 0.1 (2 - 0.7) = 0.13, x2 = 0.1417, x3 = 0.1428478, x4 = 0.14285714, and 1/7 = 0.142857142... So hardware can divide using Newton steps.

The algorithm: Step 1, choose x0 and a tolerance, plus a maximum iteration count. Step 2, compute f(x) and f'(x). Step 3, if f'(x) is zero or extremely small, stop with a warning. Step 4, x_new = x - f(x)/f'(x). Step 5, if |x_new - x| is below the tolerance (or |f(x_new)| is tiny), stop. Step 6, set x = x_new and go back to step 2. Each step costs two evaluations: f and f'.

Failure case 1, zero or flat slope: If f'(x) = 0, the tangent is horizontal and never crosses the axis; the formula divides by zero. For x^2 - 2, starting at x0 = 0 fails immediately. If f'(x) is merely small, the tangent is nearly flat and the next guess shoots far away, maybe to a different root or to nowhere.

Failure case 2, cycling: For f(x) = x^3 - 2x + 2 starting at x0 = 0: f(0) = 2, f'(0) = -2, so x1 = 1. f(1) = 1, f'(1) = 1, so x2 = 0. Back where we started! It bounces 0, 1, 0, 1 forever, even though a real root exists near -1.77. A program without a maximum iteration count would hang.

Failure case 3, bad start: For the reciprocal example with a = 7, starting at x0 = 0.3 gives x1 = 0.3 (2 - 2.1) = -0.03, which then runs off to negative numbers and diverges. For this formula the start must be between 0 and 2/a. Newton has no built-in safety net: unlike bisection, a root is not trapped anywhere.

The practical fix, hybrid methods: Real libraries usually combine safety with speed. They keep a bisection bracket, try a Newton step, and if the Newton step falls outside the bracket or does not reduce |f| enough, they take a bisection step instead. You get bisection's guarantee and Newton's speed near the root. Brent's method is a famous hybrid of this kind (it uses secant and inverse quadratic steps instead of derivatives).

Picking a starting guess: There is no magic rule, but there are good habits. Sketch the curve or tabulate f at a few points like 0, 1, 2, 3 and look for a sign change; start inside it. Use physical sense: a building height cannot be negative, an interest rate is usually a few percent. Or run three or four bisection steps first and hand the result to Newton. For square roots, even a crude guess like S/2 works, because the curve x^2 - S has no flat spots for positive x and Newton converges from any positive start there.

Mental model: Think of Newton as a very fast but slightly reckless driver with a perfect speedometer. On a smooth road near the destination, nobody beats him. On a winding road at night, starting far away, he may overshoot, turn around, and overshoot again. Bisection is the slow bus that always arrives. Good engineers let the bus bring them near the station and then switch to the fast driver for the last stretch.

Real-life example 1, GPS on your phone: When Pathao or Google Maps shows your location, the phone receives signals from several satellites and must solve a set of nonlinear equations for your position and the clock error. Receivers commonly use Newton-type iterations (the multi-variable version from lesson 10) starting from the last known position. Because the last position is close, a few steps are enough.

Real-life example 2, loan interest rate: A bank in Dhaka says: borrow 1 lakh taka, pay 9,000 taka per month for 12 months. What is the real monthly interest rate? The equation for the rate has no simple formula, so spreadsheet functions like RATE solve it with a Newton-style iteration starting from a guess such as 1 percent. A few steps give the rate to many digits.

When to use Newton-Raphson: Use it when the derivative is easy to compute, you have a reasonably good starting guess (from a graph, a physical estimate, or a few bisection steps), and you need high accuracy quickly. It is ideal inside loops that run many times, like square root routines.

When not to use it: Avoid it when the derivative is unknown, very costly, or noisy (then use secant, next lesson). Avoid it when you have no idea where the root is, near points where f' is close to zero, or at multiple roots like (x - 1)^2, where convergence slows to linear (lesson 10 covers this).

Common mistakes: Forgetting to recompute f'(x) at each new point. Using degrees instead of radians when f has sin or cos. Stopping only when |f(x)| is small, while the steps are still large because f is very flat. Not putting a maximum iteration count. And believing "Newton always converges"; it does not, it converges fast only from a good start. Another classic slip is flipping the fraction to f'(x)/f(x). A quick sanity check saves you: the step f(x)/f'(x) must have the same units as x, because f is divided by "f per unit of x".

What exams ask: Derive the formula (geometrically or by Taylor). Find a square root or cube root to four decimal places. Do three iterations of an equation like x log10(x) = 1.2 or x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0. Show that the order of convergence is 2. Give an example where it fails and draw the tangent picture.

Recap: Newton-Raphson follows the tangent line down to the axis: x_new = x - f(x)/f'(x). Near a simple root it converges quadratically, doubling correct digits each step. It needs a derivative and a good start, and it can fail by dividing by a near-zero slope, cycling, or diverging. Next lesson: the secant method, which keeps most of Newton's speed without needing the derivative.
key_points: Newton-Raphson formula: x_new = x - f(x)/f'(x), where the tangent crosses the x-axis.
It comes from keeping the first two Taylor terms: f(x0) + h f'(x0) = 0.
Near a simple root the error is squared each step (quadratic convergence), so correct digits roughly double.
For x^2 - 2 it becomes the Babylonian rule x_new = (x + 2/x)/2: 1, 1.5, 1.41667, 1.4142157, 1.4142136.
Failures: f'(x) = 0 or tiny, cycling (x^3 - 2x + 2 from 0 bounces 0, 1, 0, 1), divergence from a bad start.
Always use a maximum iteration count; real libraries combine Newton with bisection for safety.
Multiple roots make it slow (linear), and missing derivatives make secant a better choice.
lessons.tip: Before iterating, sketch f(x) roughly and pick x0 near where the curve crosses the axis. Most Newton failures come from a careless starting point, not from the formula.
lessons.task: Use a phone calculator to find the cube root of 20 with Newton: f(x) = x^3 - 20, x_new = x - (x^3 - 20)/(3x^2). Start at x0 = 3 and do three steps. Check by cubing your answer.

quiz.q: What is the Newton-Raphson update formula?
quiz.explain: The next guess is where the tangent line at x crosses the x-axis.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x^2 - 2 starting at x0 = 1, what is x2?
What does quadratic convergence mean in practice?
options: The error is roughly squared each step, so correct digits about double
The method always converges from any starting point
quiz.explain: e_new is about a constant times e_old squared, so digits roughly double near the root.

quiz.q: Newton on f(x) = x^3 - 2x + 2 from x0 = 0 gives 1, then 0, then 1 again. What is this failure called?
quiz.explain: The iterates bounce between 0 and 1 forever, so a maximum iteration count is needed.

quiz.q: Which situation is a poor fit for Newton-Raphson?
options: A cheap derivative and a good starting guess
Computing square roots in a calculator
A function whose derivative is unknown or very expensive
Refining a root already found roughly by bisection
quiz.explain: Newton needs f'(x) at every step; without it, the secant method is a better choice.

lessons.title: Secant Method: Newton Without the Derivative
lessons.content:
Think of a cricket bowler trying to land the ball exactly on a good length. His first ball pitches 2 metres too short. His second ball, with a bit more effort, pitches 1 metre too far. He does not need a physics textbook to know what to do next: somewhere between those two efforts, a little closer to the second one, is the right amount. He judges the slope from his last two attempts and adjusts. That is the secant method: learn the slope from your last two tries instead of calculating it from a formula.

What it is: The secant method is an open root-finding method for f(x) = 0. It starts from two guesses, x0 and x1, which do not need to bracket the root. It draws the straight line (a secant line) through the two points (x0, f(x0)) and (x1, f(x1)), finds where that line crosses the x-axis, and uses that as x2. Then it throws away the oldest point and repeats with x1 and x2.

The formula: x2 = x1 - f(x1) (x1 - x0) / (f(x1) - f(x0)). In general, x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) (x_n - x_(n-1)) / (f(x_n) - f(x_(n-1))). Notice it looks exactly like the false position formula. The difference is not the line, it is which two points you keep.

The problem it solves: Newton-Raphson is fast, but it needs the derivative f'(x) at every step. In real life that is often a problem. The function might come from a big program, a lab measurement, or a spreadsheet model, where nobody has a formula for the derivative. Even when a formula exists, it might be long and costly to evaluate, or easy to get wrong when you derive it by hand. The secant method replaces the derivative with something you already have: the last two function values.

Building it from Newton: Recall the definition of the derivative: f'(x) is the limit of (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h as h goes to zero. If we do not take the limit and just use two nearby points we already have, we get an approximation: f'(x_n) is roughly (f(x_n) - f(x_(n-1))) / (x_n - x_(n-1)). Put this into Newton's formula x - f(x)/f'(x) and out comes the secant formula. So secant is "Newton with a finite-difference slope".

Worked example 1, square root of 2: f(x) = x^2 - 2, start with x0 = 1 and x1 = 2. f(1) = -1, f(2) = 2. x2 = 2 - 2 (2 - 1) / (2 - (-1)) = 2 - 2/3 = 1.333333. Now use x1 = 2 and x2 = 1.333333, with f(1.333333) = -0.222222. x3 = 1.333333 - (-0.222222)(1.333333 - 2) / (-0.222222 - 2) = 1.4. Then x4 = 1.4146341, x5 = 1.4142114, x6 = 1.4142135621. The errors go 0.081, 0.014, 0.00042, 0.0000021, 0.0000000003. Very fast, without ever touching a derivative.

Worked example 2, compared with false position: Take f(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5 again with x0 = 2, x1 = 3. The first secant step is the same as false position: 2.058824. The second step uses 3 and 2.058824, and again matches false position: 2.081264. But now the paths split. False position would keep 3 because the sign change is there. Secant simply keeps the two newest points, 2.058824 and 2.081264, which are both on the same side of the root. The line through them crosses the axis at 2.094824. Next 2.0945494, then 2.0945515. After five steps secant is correct to about 9 decimal places, while false position after six steps was still wrong in the fourth decimal.

Why dropping the bracket helps: False position got stuck because one old point far away (x = 3) kept pulling the line. Secant always uses the two freshest, closest points, so the line becomes a better and better local copy of the tangent. The price is that the root is no longer trapped between them.

How fast is it: Near a simple root the secant error behaves like e_(n+1) roughly equal to C times e_n times e_(n-1). Solving this pattern gives an order of convergence p = (1 + square root of 5) / 2, about 1.618, the golden ratio. That is superlinear: faster than bisection and false position (order 1), a bit slower per step than Newton (order 2).

Speed per unit of work: Steps are not the whole story. Each Newton step costs two evaluations, f and f'. Each secant step costs only one new evaluation of f, since the older value is reused. If f' costs about as much as f, then in two evaluations Newton gains order 2, while secant does two steps and gains about 1.618 squared, roughly 2.618. So per function evaluation, the secant method is often more efficient than Newton. That is a nice example of engineering trade-off thinking: count the real cost, not just the iterations.

The algorithm: Step 1, choose x0, x1, a tolerance and a maximum iteration count. Step 2, compute f0 = f(x0), f1 = f(x1). Step 3, if f1 - f0 is zero or tiny, stop with a warning. Step 4, x2 = x1 - f1 (x1 - x0) / (f1 - f0). Step 5, if |x2 - x1| is below tolerance, return x2. Step 6, shift: x0 = x1, f0 = f1, x1 = x2, f1 = f(x2). Go to step 3. A good program stores f values, so only one new function call happens per loop.

Failure case 1, flat line: If f(x1) and f(x0) are nearly equal, the secant line is almost horizontal and the next guess jumps far away. If they are exactly equal, the formula divides by zero. This is the secant version of Newton's f' = 0 problem.

Failure case 2, losing the root: Because secant does not keep a bracket, nothing stops it from wandering away if the starting points are poor or the function has wiggles. It can diverge, or converge to a different root than the one you wanted. As with Newton, safe software wraps it inside a bracketing method; Brent's method combines bisection, secant and inverse quadratic interpolation for exactly this reason.

Failure case 3, round-off near the end: When x1 and x0 are extremely close, f(x1) - f(x0) is a subtraction of two nearly equal numbers. As you saw in the lessons on error, this loses significant digits. In practice you stop as soon as the change is below your tolerance, before the difference turns into noise.

Choosing the two starting points: The two points should be close to the root and not have nearly equal f values. A simple habit is to tabulate f at a few values, find where it changes sign, and use the two values on either side as x0 and x1. The first step is then identical to a false position step, which is safe. After that you let secant run freely. If you have only one guess x0, a common trick is x1 = x0 times 1.01, or x0 plus a small step, so the first slope is a fair local estimate.

Checking your answer: Whatever method you use, plug the final x back into the original equation. For x = 2.0945515 in x^3 - 2x - 5, the left side comes out around zero to six or seven decimals. If the residual is big, something went wrong: a typo in f, a wrong sign in the formula, or convergence to a different root. Also look at the sequence of changes |x_(n+1) - x_n|. For secant they should shrink faster and faster; if they grow or bounce, stop and rethink the starting points.

Three methods side by side: Bisection: needs a bracket, uses signs only, order 1 with factor exactly one half, never fails. False position: needs a bracket, uses the chord, order 1 (can stagnate), never loses the root. Secant: needs two starting points, no bracket, uses the chord of the two newest points, order about 1.618, can diverge. Newton: needs one point and f', uses the tangent, order 2, can diverge. Memorize this table through its reasons, not by heart: bracket means safe, local information means fast.

Mental model: Picture walking down a dark staircase. Newton has a torch that shows the exact steepness right at his feet. Secant has no torch but remembers how much he dropped over his last step, and assumes the next step is similar. Near the bottom, where steps are regular, memory is almost as good as the torch, and much cheaper.

Real-life example 1, a business model in a spreadsheet: A small garments exporter in Gazipur has a big Excel sheet that takes the unit price and computes yearly profit through many linked formulas. They want the price where profit is exactly zero. Nobody can write the derivative of that whole sheet. They try 300 taka (loss of 2 lakh) and 350 taka (profit of 1 lakh). Secant gives 350 - 1 (50) / (1 - (-2)) = 333.33 taka as the next try. Excel's Goal Seek feature does this kind of iterative search for you.

Real-life example 2, aiming a water hose: A firefighter in Old Dhaka wants the water to hit a window. At one nozzle angle the stream lands 3 metres low, at another it lands 1 metre high. The next angle is chosen on the line between those two results. In numerical methods this is called the shooting method for boundary value problems, and secant is the usual way to update the aim, because each "shot" is an expensive simulation without a simple derivative.

When to use secant: Use it when f is smooth, you have two reasonable starting values near the root, the derivative is unavailable or expensive, and you want speed close to Newton. It is a great default for black-box functions where each evaluation is costly.

When not to use it: Avoid it alone when you must guarantee convergence (use bisection or a hybrid), when f is noisy so differences of nearby values are meaningless, or when the function has nearly equal values at your starting points.

Common mistakes: Mixing it up with false position and keeping the bracket (then you get false position, not secant). Using the same point twice so the denominator is zero. Recomputing old f values each step and doubling the cost. Writing the order as 2; it is about 1.618.

What exams ask: Derive the secant formula from Newton's formula. Perform three or four iterations on equations like x^3 - 5x + 1 = 0 or x e^x - cos x = 0. State the order of convergence (1.618). Explain the difference between secant and regula falsi with a sketch. Compare bisection, false position, secant and Newton.

Recap: The secant method is Newton's method with the derivative replaced by the slope through the last two points: x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n)(x_n - x_(n-1)) / (f(x_n) - f(x_(n-1))). It needs no derivative, converges with order about 1.618, and is often the cheapest per function evaluation, but without a bracket it can diverge. Next we look at a different family entirely: rewriting f(x) = 0 as x = g(x) and iterating.
key_points: Secant formula: x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n)(x_n - x_(n-1)) / (f(x_n) - f(x_(n-1))).
It is Newton's method with f'(x) replaced by the slope through the last two points.
Same line as false position, but secant always keeps the two newest points, not a bracket.
Order of convergence is about 1.618 (the golden ratio), superlinear.
Only one new function evaluation per step, so per evaluation it is often more efficient than Newton.
It can diverge, divide by zero when f(x_n) = f(x_(n-1)), or lose digits when points get very close.
lessons.tip: When you compare root methods, always ask two questions: does it keep a bracket (safety), and how much local information does it use (speed). Every difference in the comparison table comes from these two.
lessons.task: Using a calculator, do four secant steps for f(x) = x^2 - 5 starting at x0 = 2 and x1 = 3. Then do four bisection steps on [2, 3] and see how much closer secant gets to 2.23607.

quiz.q: How does the secant method avoid needing the derivative?
options: It uses the midpoint of the interval
It approximates f'(x) by the slope through the last two points
It uses the second derivative instead
quiz.explain: The finite-difference slope (f(x_n) - f(x_(n-1)))/(x_n - x_(n-1)) replaces f'(x_n).

quiz.q: What is the main difference between the secant method and false position?
options: Secant always keeps the two newest points, while false position keeps a sign-change bracket
False position is an open method
quiz.explain: Same chord formula, but secant drops the bracket, which makes it faster and less safe.

quiz.q: What is the order of convergence of the secant method near a simple root?
quiz.explain: It is the golden ratio (1 + sqrt 5)/2, between linear and quadratic.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x^2 - 2 with x0 = 1 and x1 = 2, what is x2 from the secant method?
Why can secant be more efficient than Newton per unit of work?
options: Each step needs only one new function evaluation instead of f and f'
quiz.explain: Two secant steps cost about the same as one Newton step and give a combined order near 2.618.

lessons.title: Fixed-Point Iteration: Feeding the Answer Back In
lessons.content:
Here is a fun experiment you can do on any calculator right now. Make sure it is in radian mode. Type any number, say 1, and press the cos button. Then press cos again. And again. And again. After twenty or thirty presses the screen stops changing and settles at 0.739085... Whatever number you start with, you end up at the same place. You have just solved the equation x = cos x, a problem with no neat algebra formula, by pressing one button. That is fixed-point iteration.

What a fixed point is: A fixed point of a function g is a number r with g(r) = r. Put r into the machine, and r comes out unchanged. For g(x) = cos x, the fixed point is about 0.739085, because cos(0.739085) = 0.739085. For g(x) = x^2, both 0 and 1 are fixed points, since 0^2 = 0 and 1^2 = 1.

What the method is: Fixed-point iteration solves f(x) = 0 in two moves. First, rewrite the equation in the form x = g(x). Second, start with a guess x0 and repeat x_(n+1) = g(x_n). If the numbers settle down, they settle at a fixed point of g, which is a root of f. Nothing more: no bracket, no derivative, just "plug the answer back in". The Babylonian square root rule from the last lessons, x_new = (x + S/x)/2, is itself a fixed-point iteration, and a very good one.

Why it matters: Fixed-point iteration is the simplest open method, and more importantly it is the language for understanding almost every iterative method. Newton's method, the Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel methods for linear systems (lesson 15), even the way some economic models and Google's original PageRank are computed, are all "keep applying a map until nothing changes". Learn when a fixed-point iteration converges, and you understand the heart of all of them.

Rewriting the equation: The tricky part is that one equation can be rewritten in many ways. Take f(x) = x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0, whose roots are 3 and -1, since (x - 3)(x + 1) = 0. Rewrite 1: x^2 = 2x + 3, so x = square root of (2x + 3). Rewrite 2: 2x = x^2 - 3, so x = (x^2 - 3)/2. Rewrite 3: x(x - 2) = 3, so x = 3/(x - 2). All three are correct algebra. All three have 3 or -1 as fixed points. Now let us see what happens when we iterate.

Trying rewrite 1: g(x) = square root of (2x + 3), start x0 = 4. x1 = sqrt(11) = 3.31662. x2 = 3.10375. x3 = 3.03439. x4 = 3.01144. x5 = 3.00381. x6 = 3.00127. Beautiful: it walks steadily to 3. The errors are 0.317, 0.104, 0.034, 0.0114, 0.0038, 0.0013. Each error is about one third of the one before.

Trying rewrite 2: g(x) = (x^2 - 3)/2, start x0 = 4. x1 = 6.5. x2 = 19.625. x3 = 191.07. x4 = 18252.4. It explodes. Same equation, same starting point, completely useless rearrangement. So the method does not just depend on the equation, it depends on how you write g.

Trying rewrite 3: g(x) = 3/(x - 2), start x0 = 4. x1 = 1.5. x2 = -6. x3 = -0.375. x4 = -1.263. x5 = -0.919. x6 = -1.028. It ignores the nearby root 3 and slowly zigzags toward the other root, -1, jumping above and below it each time.

The rule that explains everything: Near a fixed point r, write x_n = r + e_n, where e_n is the error. Then x_(n+1) = g(r + e_n), and by Taylor that is about g(r) + g'(r) e_n = r + g'(r) e_n. So e_(n+1) is about g'(r) times e_n. The error gets multiplied by g'(r) every step! If |g'(r)| < 1, the error shrinks and the iteration converges. If |g'(r)| > 1, the error grows and it diverges. That single fact, |g'(r)| < 1, is the convergence condition.

Checking our three rewrites: Rewrite 1: g'(x) = 1/sqrt(2x + 3), so g'(3) = 1/3. Less than 1, so it converges, and the error shrinks by a factor of about 1/3, exactly what we saw. Rewrite 2: g'(x) = x, so g'(3) = 3. Bigger than 1, error triples, it diverges. Rewrite 3: g'(x) = -3/(x - 2)^2, so g'(3) = -3, which repels from 3, but g'(-1) = -3/9 = -1/3, so -1 attracts it. The minus sign explains the zigzag: the error flips sign each step. For x = cos x, g'(x) = -sin x and at the fixed point sin(0.739) is about 0.674, so it converges, zigzagging, but slowly.

The cobweb picture: Draw the line y = x and the curve y = g(x). They meet at the fixed point. Start at x0 on the x-axis, go up to the curve (that is g(x0) = x1), then sideways to the line y = x (which moves x1 to the x-axis position), then up or down to the curve again, and so on. If the curve is flatter than the line near the crossing (|slope| < 1), the path spirals or staircases inward. If it is steeper, it spirals outward. Positive slope gives a staircase; negative slope gives a spiral, like a cobweb. Exam papers love this diagram.

A stronger guarantee: The fixed-point theorem says: if g maps an interval [a, b] into itself, and |g'(x)| <= k < 1 for all x in that interval, then g has exactly one fixed point there, and the iteration converges to it from any starting point in [a, b]. It even gives a bound: the error after n steps is at most k^n / (1 - k) times |x1 - x0|. So you can tell in advance how many steps you need.

Rate and order of convergence: Order tells how the new error relates to the old. Linear (order 1): e_new is about C times e_old, with C < 1. Quadratic (order 2): e_new is about C times e_old squared. Ordinary fixed-point iteration is linear with C = |g'(r)|; smaller is faster. With C = 1/3 you gain about half a decimal digit per step; with C = 0.674 for cos x you gain less than a fifth of a digit per step.

The algorithm: Step 1, rewrite f(x) = 0 as x = g(x) and check |g'(x)| < 1 near the expected root. Step 2, choose x0, a tolerance and a maximum number of iterations. Step 3, compute x_new = g(x). Step 4, if |x_new - x| is below the tolerance, stop. Step 5, set x = x_new and go back to step 3. Each step costs exactly one evaluation of g, and the program only has to remember one number, the current x. That is why this method is so popular in tiny devices and in hand calculations.

Making your own good rearrangement: If no natural rearrangement works, there is a general trick. Write g(x) = x - c f(x) for some constant c. Its fixed points are still the roots of f, because g(x) = x exactly when f(x) = 0. Now g'(r) = 1 - c f'(r). Choose c close to 1/f'(r), using a rough estimate of the slope near the root, and g'(r) becomes close to 0, so the iteration converges fast. If you keep updating c to 1/f'(x) at every step, you have reinvented Newton's method.

Mental model: Think of a rumour about the price of onions passing from shop to shop in a bazar. Each shopkeeper hears a price and passes on a slightly adjusted version. If every shopkeeper only changes it a little toward the true price (|g'| < 1), the rumour settles at one stable price. If each one exaggerates the difference (|g'| > 1), the rumour gets wilder and wilder. A fixed point is the price that, when passed on, comes back unchanged.

The secret about Newton: Newton's method is a fixed-point iteration with g(x) = x - f(x)/f'(x). If you work out g'(x), you get f(x) f''(x) / f'(x)^2, which is zero at a simple root because f(r) = 0. With g'(r) = 0, the linear error term disappears and only the squared term is left. That is exactly why Newton is quadratic. So the best possible rearrangement is one whose slope at the root is zero.

The order table: Bisection: linear, factor exactly 1/2. False position: linear (factor depends on the curve). Fixed point: linear, factor |g'(r)|. Secant: about 1.618. Newton: 2. Remember the reasons: bracketing methods are linear, using a chord gives 1.618, using an exact tangent gives 2.

Real-life example 1, grossing up a salary: A company in Dhaka wants an employee to receive exactly 50,000 taka in hand after a 10% deduction taken from the gross. So gross x must satisfy x = 50,000 + 0.1x. Iterate g(x) = 50,000 + 0.1x from 50,000: 55,000, then 55,500, then 55,550, then 55,555. The exact answer is 55,555.56. Here g'(x) = 0.1, so each step gains one digit, which is why it converges so fast. Payroll and tax calculations where the amount depends on itself are often solved this way.

Real-life example 2, ranking web pages: Google's original PageRank gives each page a score that depends on the scores of pages linking to it. The score vector is the fixed point of a map, and it is computed by applying the map again and again until the scores stop changing. A damping factor of about 0.85 was used, which keeps the map contracting so the iteration converges.

When to use fixed-point iteration: Use it when a natural rearrangement x = g(x) exists with |g'| clearly below 1 near the root, when g is cheap, and when simple code matters more than speed. It is also the right mental tool to analyze any iterative method.

When not to use it: Avoid it when you cannot find a rearrangement with |g'| < 1, when |g'(r)| is close to 1 (painfully slow), or when you need high accuracy fast; then Newton or secant is better.

Common mistakes: Checking |g'(x0)| at the starting point only and forgetting it must hold near the root. Checking |f'| instead of |g'|. Assuming every algebraically correct rearrangement works. Calculator in degree mode for cos x. Stopping when two iterates differ by less than the tolerance when C is close to 1; then the true error can be much bigger than the change (the bound k/(1 - k) times the last change tells you how much bigger).

What exams ask: Rewrite an equation like x^3 + x^2 - 1 = 0 into x = g(x) forms, test |g'(x)| < 1, and iterate four or five times. State and explain the convergence condition. Draw cobweb diagrams for converging and diverging cases. Show that Newton is a fixed-point iteration with g'(r) = 0.

Recap: Rewrite f(x) = 0 as x = g(x) and iterate x_(n+1) = g(x_n). Near the root the error is multiplied by g'(r) each step, so it converges if |g'(r)| < 1, linearly, faster when |g'(r)| is smaller, and quadratically when g'(r) = 0, which is Newton. Next lesson: special tools for polynomials and for several equations at once.
key_points: A fixed point r of g satisfies g(r) = r; rewrite f(x) = 0 as x = g(x) and iterate x_(n+1) = g(x_n).
The same equation can be rearranged many ways; some converge, some explode.
Near the root the error is multiplied by g'(r) each step, so it converges when |g'(r)| < 1.
x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0: x = sqrt(2x + 3) converges to 3 (g' = 1/3); x = (x^2 - 3)/2 diverges (g' = 3).
Negative g' gives a zigzag (spiral cobweb); positive g' gives a staircase.
Fixed-point iteration is linear with rate |g'(r)|; Newton is the special case with g'(r) = 0, hence quadratic.
Order table: bisection 1, false position 1, fixed point 1, secant about 1.618, Newton 2.
lessons.tip: Before iterating any x = g(x), compute g'(x) near the root and check its size. Ten seconds of differentiation saves you from ten useless iterations.
lessons.task: In radian mode, press cos repeatedly starting from 0, then from 3, and count how many presses it takes to reach 0.7391. Then try the button for square root starting from 50 and explain, using g'(x), why it settles at 1.

quiz.q: What is the convergence condition for fixed-point iteration near a root r?
quiz.explain: The error is multiplied by g'(r) each step, so it must have size less than 1 to shrink.

quiz.q: For x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0, which rearrangement converges to the root 3?
quiz.explain: Its derivative at 3 is 1/3, below 1; the first two have |g'(3)| = 3.

quiz.q: What does a negative g'(r) with |g'(r)| < 1 look like during iteration?
options: A steady staircase from one side
Iterates zigzag above and below the root while converging
The iteration stops after one step
quiz.explain: The error changes sign every step, which draws a spiral cobweb.

quiz.q: Why is Newton's method quadratic when viewed as fixed-point iteration?
options: Because g'(r) = 0 at a simple root, so the linear error term vanishes
Because it needs two starting points
quiz.explain: With g(x) = x - f/f', g'(r) = f f''/f'^2 = 0 at the root, leaving the squared error term.

quiz.q: Iterating g(x) = 50000 + 0.1x from 50000 gives 55000, 55500, 55550. Why does it converge so fast?
options: g'(x) = 0.1, so each step cuts the error by a factor of 10
quiz.explain: A small |g'| means a small error multiplier: about one more correct digit per step.

lessons.title: Roots of Polynomials and Systems of Nonlinear Equations
lessons.content:
So far we have chased one root of one equation. Real problems are often greedier. An engineer may want all the roots of a polynomial, because each root describes one vibration mode of a bridge. A GPS receiver must find several unknowns at once, position and clock error, from several equations that all depend on each other. This lesson gives you four tools for those jobs: Horner's method to evaluate polynomials quickly, deflation to find root after root, a fix for multiple roots where Newton slows down, and Newton's method for systems of equations.

Why polynomials get special treatment: Polynomials like p(x) = 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 1 appear everywhere: in curve fitting, in control systems, in the characteristic equations of matrices, and inside the interpolation formulas of later lessons. They are so common that it pays to evaluate them as cheaply and accurately as possible, and they have a useful property: once you know one root r, you can divide by (x - r) and get a smaller polynomial holding the remaining roots.

The naive way to evaluate: To compute 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 1 directly, you calculate x^3 (two multiplications), multiply by 2, compute x^2, multiply by 6, multiply 2 by x, then add everything. For a polynomial of degree n, done this way, the number of multiplications grows roughly like n^2 / 2 if you compute each power from scratch. Every multiplication costs time and adds a little round-off error.

Horner's method: Rewrite the polynomial by pulling x out again and again: 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 1 = ((2x - 6)x + 2)x - 1. Now evaluation is a simple loop: start with the leading coefficient, then repeatedly multiply by x and add the next coefficient. For degree n that is exactly n multiplications and n additions, which is the minimum possible for a general polynomial. In code: b = a[0]; for each next coefficient c: b = b times x plus c. Fewer operations also means fewer chances for round-off error to creep in, so Horner is both faster and usually more accurate.

Horner worked example: Evaluate p(3) for p(x) = 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 1. Coefficients: 2, -6, 2, -1. Start b = 2. Multiply by 3 and add -6: 6 - 6 = 0. Multiply by 3 and add 2: 0 + 2 = 2. Multiply by 3 and add -1: 6 - 1 = 5. So p(3) = 5. Check directly: 54 - 54 + 6 - 1 = 5. Correct, and with only three multiplications.

The bonus hidden in Horner: The intermediate numbers 2, 0, 2 are not junk. They are the coefficients of the quotient when p(x) is divided by (x - 3): p(x) = (x - 3)(2x^2 + 0x + 2) + 5. This is the same as synthetic division you may have learned in school. The last number, 5, is the remainder, which equals p(3). Run Horner again on the quotient 2, 0, 2 with x = 3: 2, then 6 + 0 = 6, then 18 + 2 = 20. That 20 is p'(3). Check: p'(x) = 6x^2 - 12x + 2, so p'(3) = 54 - 36 + 2 = 20. Two cheap passes give you both p(x) and p'(x), exactly what Newton's method needs.

Newton for a polynomial with Horner: Starting at x0 = 3 for our p: x1 = 3 - 5/20 = 2.75. Repeating gives 2.7, then 2.698051, then 2.6980481. The real root of 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 1 is about 2.698048. This combination, Newton with Horner for evaluation, is the classic Birge-Vieta method taught in many syllabi.

Deflation: Once you find a root r, divide p(x) by (x - r) using the Horner pass, and continue with the quotient. Example: p(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6. Trying x = 1: Horner gives 1, then 1 - 6 = -5, then -5 + 11 = 6, then 6 - 6 = 0. Remainder 0, so 1 is a root, and the quotient is x^2 - 5x + 6. That quadratic has roots 2 and 3 by the usual formula. So p has roots 1, 2, 3, and we never had to search the full cubic again.

The danger in deflation: In real computation the root r is only approximate, so the quotient is slightly wrong. Each deflation passes its error on to the next polynomial, and errors can pile up. Two good habits limit this. First, find and remove roots of smallest size first, which is usually more stable. Second, after you have all approximate roots, polish each one by running a couple of Newton steps on the original polynomial, not the deflated one.

Multiple roots, the problem: A root r is multiple when the curve touches the axis without crossing, like (x - 1)^2, where both f and f' are zero at r. Newton divides f by f', and both go to zero together. Try f(x) = (x - 1)^2 = x^2 - 2x + 1 starting at 2: the iterates are 1.5, 1.25, 1.125, 1.0625, 1.03125. The error just halves each step. Newton has dropped from quadratic to linear, no better than bisection. Also, bisection cannot even start here, because f does not change sign at a double root.

Multiple roots, the fixes: If you know the multiplicity m (how many times the root repeats), use modified Newton: x_new = x - m f(x)/f'(x). For (x - 1)^2 with m = 2 starting at 2: x_new = 2 - 2(1)/2 = 1, the exact root in one step. If you do not know m, apply Newton to u(x) = f(x)/f'(x) instead of f. The function u has a simple root at r, so quadratic speed returns, at the cost of needing f'' as well. In practice, a sudden slow linear crawl in Newton is a strong hint that you are near a multiple root.

Why multiple roots matter in reality: A double root is a borderline case: a tiny change in the coefficients can split it into two close real roots or into two complex roots. That makes such roots sensitive to round-off, just like the ill-conditioned linear systems you will meet in lesson 12. Engineers watch for them because they often mark a design right on the edge between two behaviours.

Systems of nonlinear equations: Now suppose two unknowns and two equations, for example x^2 + y^2 = 4 (a circle of radius 2) and xy = 1 (a hyperbola). The solutions are the points where the curves cross. No single-variable trick works because each equation contains both unknowns. We need Newton in more than one dimension.

Newton for systems, the idea: For one equation Newton replaced the curve by its tangent line. For two equations we replace each surface by its tangent plane, using all partial derivatives. Collect them in the Jacobian matrix J. For f1 = x^2 + y^2 - 4 and f2 = xy - 1, J has rows (2x, 2y) and (y, x). Each step solves the linear system J times (dx, dy) = -(f1, f2) and updates x = x + dx, y = y + dy. So every Newton step on a nonlinear system is one linear system solve, which is why the next five lessons on linear systems matter so much.

Worked example: Start at (2, 0.5). Then f1 = 4 + 0.25 - 4 = 0.25 and f2 = 1 - 1 = 0. J = [[4, 1], [0.5, 2]]. Solve 4 dx + dy = -0.25 and 0.5 dx + 2 dy = 0. From the second, dx = -4 dy. Put it into the first: -16 dy + dy = -0.25, so dy = 1/60 = 0.016667 and dx = -0.066667. New point (1.933333, 0.516667). One more step gives (1.931853, 0.517637). The exact solution is ((square root 6 + square root 2)/2, (square root 6 - square root 2)/2), which is (1.9318517, 0.5176381). Two steps, six correct digits: the quadratic speed survives in higher dimensions.

The cost and the catches: For n unknowns, each step needs n^2 partial derivatives and a linear solve costing about (2/3)n^3 operations. If the Jacobian is singular (determinant zero) the step is undefined, the multi-dimensional version of f' = 0. And a good starting point matters even more than in one dimension, because there are more directions to go wrong. Quasi-Newton methods such as Broyden's update the Jacobian approximately, like secant does for one variable, to save cost.

Real-life example 1, GPS positioning: Your phone measures the travel time of signals from at least four satellites. Each gives an equation like "distance from me to satellite k equals speed of light times measured time, after correcting my clock error". Four equations, four unknowns (x, y, z, clock error), all nonlinear because distance has a square root. Receivers linearize and iterate, Newton-style (usually in a least-squares form), from the previous fix. That is how Pathao finds your pickup point.

Real-life example 2, power flow in the national grid: Engineers at power companies in Bangladesh plan how much electricity flows on each line by solving the "load flow" equations: hundreds or thousands of nonlinear equations linking voltages and powers at every substation. The standard industrial method is Newton-Raphson load flow, with a large sparse Jacobian solved at every iteration.

When to use these tools: Horner always, whenever you evaluate a polynomial. Deflation when you need all roots of a modest-degree polynomial and you polish afterwards. Modified Newton when you see a multiple root. Newton for systems when equations are smooth, the Jacobian is available, and you have a decent start.

When not to: For high-degree polynomials with many roots, including complex ones, specialised methods such as finding eigenvalues of the companion matrix are more reliable; that is how many software libraries' polynomial root functions work. Avoid plain Newton for systems from a wild starting point, and avoid deflating with low-accuracy roots without polishing.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to include zero coefficients in Horner, for example writing 2x^3 + 5 as 2, 5 instead of 2, 0, 0, 5. Using deflated polynomials for the final answer without polishing. Calling Newton broken when it is just slowed by a double root. In systems, mixing up rows and columns of the Jacobian, or solving J d = f instead of J d = -f.

What exams ask: Evaluate a polynomial and its derivative by synthetic division, then do Birge-Vieta iterations. Deflate a cubic after one root. Explain why Newton converges linearly at a double root and give the modified formula. Do one or two Newton steps for a pair of equations such as x^2 + y^2 = 4, xy = 1, writing the Jacobian.

Recap: Horner evaluates a degree-n polynomial in n multiplications and, run twice, gives p and p'. Deflation removes found roots but spreads error, so polish at the end. At a multiple root Newton becomes linear; multiply the step by m or use f/f'. For systems, Newton uses the Jacobian and solves a linear system each step, keeping quadratic speed near the solution. That linear solve is our next big topic: Gauss elimination.
key_points: Horner: write a polynomial as nested multiplications; degree n needs only n multiplications and n additions.
Horner's intermediate values give the quotient after dividing by (x - r); a second pass gives p'(x).
Deflation divides out a found root; it spreads error, so polish roots on the original polynomial.
At a multiple root Newton becomes linear; modified Newton x - m f/f' restores speed.
Newton for systems solves J d = -F each step using the Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives.
From (2, 0.5), x^2 + y^2 = 4 and xy = 1 reach (1.931853, 0.517637) in two steps.
lessons.tip: In synthetic division always write every coefficient, including zeros for missing powers, in one row. Most wrong answers in Horner problems come from a missing zero.
lessons.task: Use Horner by hand to evaluate p(x) = x^4 - 3x^3 + 0x^2 + 5x - 2 at x = 2, then run Horner again on the quotient to get p'(2). Check both answers by direct substitution.

quiz.q: How many multiplications does Horner's method need to evaluate a general polynomial of degree n?
quiz.explain: Each of the n steps does one multiply and one add, the minimum for a general polynomial.

quiz.q: Using Horner on p(x) = 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 1 at x = 3, what are p(3) and p'(3)?
quiz.explain: First pass gives 2, 0, 2, 5 so p(3) = 5; second pass on 2, 0, 2 gives 2, 6, 20.

quiz.q: What happens to Newton's method at a double root like (x - 1)^2?
options: It converges linearly, the error roughly halving each step
quiz.explain: Both f and f' vanish at the root, so the convergence drops from quadratic to linear.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of deflation?
options: Errors in approximate roots carry into the deflated polynomial and can pile up
It cannot be done with Horner's method

J d = F with J the identity matrix

lessons.title: Linear Systems and Gauss Elimination
lessons.content:
Imagine three friends at a tea stall in Mirpur. Rafi buys 2 cups of tea and 1 singara and pays 30 taka. Mitu buys 1 cup of tea and 2 singaras and pays 30 taka too. What does one tea cost, and what does one singara cost? Neither fact alone tells you, but together they do: tea is 10 taka and singara is 10 taka. Very often we know several facts that each mix a few unknown numbers together, and we want all the unknowns at once. That is a system of linear equations. Until now in this course we solved one equation with one unknown, like finding x where f(x) = 0. Now we move to many equations with many unknowns, and that is where most real engineering computing actually happens.

What a linear system is: A linear equation is one where every unknown appears only to the power 1, multiplied by a number, and added up. 2x + y - z = 8 is linear. x times y = 3 is not, and neither is x^2 + y = 5. A linear system is a group of such equations that must all be true at the same time. If you have n unknowns, you usually need n independent equations to pin down one exact answer. With 2 unknowns you can picture it: each equation is a straight line, and the answer is where the lines cross.

Matrix form, Ax = b: Writing every equation in full gets messy, so we pack the numbers into a box. A is the coefficient matrix, holding the numbers in front of the unknowns. x is the column of unknowns. b is the column of right-hand sides. For our example system 2x + y - z = 8, -3x - y + 2z = -11, -2x + y + 2z = -3, the matrix A has rows (2, 1, -1), (-3, -1, 2), (-2, 1, 2), and b is (8, -11, -3). The augmented matrix [A | b] just glues b on as an extra column, so all the information sits in one table that a computer can store as a 2D array.

Where these systems come from: Electrical circuits give one equation per loop or node (Kirchhoff's laws, which you saw in Electrical Circuits). Building and bridge design splits a structure into many small pieces, and every piece gives equations about forces. Weather and flood models split the land into grid cells, and each cell talks to its neighbours through equations. Machine learning's least squares fitting ends in a linear system too, as you will see in lesson 20. Real systems can have thousands or even millions of unknowns, so we need a method a computer can run without any human cleverness.

What people did before, and why it is not enough: In school you may have learned Cramer's rule: each unknown equals one determinant divided by another determinant. It is beautiful for 2 or 3 unknowns. But if you compute determinants by the cofactor expansion you learned in school, the work grows like n factorial. For n = 20, that is about 2.4 times 10^18 multiplications, which would take a fast laptop years. Another school idea is x = A inverse times b. Finding the inverse costs about three times more work than simply solving the system, and it also adds more round-off error. So for real computing we need something smarter: elimination.

The key idea of elimination: You are allowed to do three things to the equations without changing the answer. Swap two equations. Multiply an equation by a non-zero number. Add a multiple of one equation to another equation. Why is the answer unchanged? If x, y, z make both equations true, they also make any combination of those equations true, and each step can be undone. Gauss elimination uses these moves in a fixed, boring, mechanical order, which is exactly what a computer loves.

Two phases: Gauss elimination has two phases. Phase 1 is forward elimination: use the first equation to remove x from every equation below it, then use the second equation to remove y from every equation below it, and so on. At the end the matrix is upper triangular, meaning all numbers below the main diagonal are zero. Phase 2 is back substitution: the last equation now has only one unknown, so solve it, plug it into the equation above, solve that, and keep climbing up.

Pivot and multiplier: In each step, the number on the diagonal that we use to kill the numbers below it is called the pivot. To clear the number in row i, we compute the multiplier m = (number to clear) / (pivot) and then do row i = row i - m times pivot row. That subtraction makes the target exactly zero, because number - (number / pivot) times pivot = 0.

Worked example, step 1: Take the augmented matrix with rows (2, 1, -1 | 8), (-3, -1, 2 | -11), (-2, 1, 2 | -3). The first pivot is 2. For row 2, the multiplier is -3 / 2 = -1.5. Row 2 minus (-1.5) times row 1 means row 2 plus 1.5 times row 1: (-3 + 3, -1 + 1.5, 2 - 1.5 | -11 + 12) = (0, 0.5, 0.5 | 1). For row 3, the multiplier is -2 / 2 = -1, so row 3 plus row 1: (0, 2, 1 | 5). Now x has vanished from rows 2 and 3.

Worked example, step 2: The new pivot is 0.5, sitting in row 2, column 2. For row 3, the multiplier is 2 / 0.5 = 4. Row 3 minus 4 times row 2: (0, 2 - 2, 1 - 2 | 5 - 4) = (0, 0, -1 | 1). The matrix is now upper triangular: (2, 1, -1 | 8), (0, 0.5, 0.5 | 1), (0, 0, -1 | 1).

Worked example, back substitution: The last row says -z = 1, so z = -1. The middle row says 0.5y + 0.5z = 1, so 0.5y - 0.5 = 1, which gives 0.5y = 1.5 and y = 3. The top row says 2x + y - z = 8, so 2x + 3 + 1 = 8, 2x = 4 and x = 2. Always check by plugging back into an original equation: -3(2) - 3 + 2(-1) = -6 - 3 - 2 = -11. Correct.

What happens inside the computer: The matrix is stored as an n by n array. Forward elimination is three nested loops: for each pivot column k, for each row i below k, compute m = a[i][k] / a[k][k], then for each column j from k to the end, a[i][j] = a[i][j] - m * a[k][j]. The same subtraction is applied to b. Back substitution is two loops going from the bottom row upward: x[i] = (b[i] - sum of a[i][j] * x[j] for j after i) / a[i][i]. Notice we can overwrite the original array in place, so no extra memory is needed beyond the matrix itself.

How much work it takes: Counting the inner subtraction across all three loops gives about (2/3) n^3 floating point operations for elimination, while back substitution needs only about n^2. So for big n, elimination dominates. For n = 1,000 unknowns that is around 670 million operations, under a second on a modern laptop. Compare that with the factorial explosion of cofactor-based Cramer's rule, and you see why Gauss elimination won. Still, n^3 grows fast: doubling n makes the work about 8 times bigger.

When the method breaks: If a pivot turns out to be exactly zero, the multiplier needs division by zero and the method stops. Sometimes swapping rows fixes it; this is called pivoting and it gets the whole next lesson. If no swap can give a non-zero pivot, the matrix is singular: the equations either contradict each other (no solution, like parallel lines) or repeat each other (infinitely many solutions, like the same line drawn twice). In that case one row becomes all zeros on the left side, and the right side tells you which situation you are in: 0 = 0 means infinite solutions, 0 = 5 means no solution.

Real-life example 1, a shop's daily mix: A small shop in Chattogram sells three packs of dal, rice and oil. On Saturday they sold 2 packs of A, 1 of B and 1 of C for 4 hundred taka; on Sunday 4, 3 and 3 for 10 hundred taka; on Monday 8, 7 and 9 for 24 hundred taka. The owner wants the price of each pack. That is a 3 by 3 linear system, and Gauss elimination gives 1 hundred taka for each pack. A spreadsheet's solver does exactly these row operations behind the scenes.

Real-life example 2, a circuit: In a simple electric circuit with three loops, Kirchhoff's voltage law gives one equation per loop, with the three loop currents as unknowns. Engineers at a factory checking a control panel do not solve these by hand; circuit simulation programs build the matrix A from the resistors and the vector b from the batteries, then run elimination. A large chip simulation can have many thousands of such equations.

When to use Gauss elimination: Use it for small to medium dense systems, meaning most entries of A are non-zero, up to maybe several thousand unknowns on a normal computer. It gives the answer in a fixed number of steps, with no guessing and no convergence worries. It is the default method inside most library solvers, usually in its LU form, which you will meet in lesson 14.

When not to use it: If you have to solve many systems with the same A and different b, redoing the full elimination each time is wasteful; LU decomposition stores the work. If A is huge and sparse, mostly zeros like the grid models with millions of cells, elimination fills those zeros with non-zero numbers and memory explodes; iterative methods like Gauss-Seidel in lesson 15 are better there. And if your system is nonlinear, elimination alone does not apply.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting to apply the row operation to the right-hand side b. Second, sign slips: subtracting a negative multiplier means adding. Third, starting back substitution from the top instead of the bottom. Fourth, dividing by a pivot that is zero or very tiny without swapping rows. Fifth, not checking the answer by substitution, which takes ten seconds and catches almost every arithmetic slip.

What exams ask: Expect "Solve this 3 by 3 system by Gauss elimination and show every step", "What is a pivot and a multiplier?", "Why is Cramer's rule not used for large systems?", "How many operations does Gauss elimination need?" with the answer about (2/3) n^3, and "What happens if a pivot is zero?". Write the augmented matrix after every step so the examiner can follow you.

Mental model: Think of a ladder of equations. Forward elimination knocks out one unknown per rung as you go down, until the bottom rung holds just one unknown. Back substitution then climbs back up, and at every rung exactly one new unknown is revealed. If you can picture that staircase shape, the upper triangular matrix, you understand Gauss elimination.

Recap: A linear system is many linear equations true at the same time, written as Ax = b. Gauss elimination uses legal row operations to make A upper triangular, then solves from the bottom up. It costs about (2/3) n^3 operations, far cheaper than cofactor determinants or computing an inverse. It fails on zero pivots, which leads us straight into the next lesson on pivoting.
key_points: A linear system is several linear equations that must hold together, written Ax = b with augmented matrix [A | b].
Row swaps, scaling a row, and adding a multiple of one row to another never change the solution.
Forward elimination makes A upper triangular using pivots and multipliers m = a[i][k] / a[k][k].
Back substitution solves from the last equation upward.
Gauss elimination costs about (2/3) n^3 operations; back substitution only about n^2.
Cramer's rule with cofactor determinants grows like n factorial, so it is useless for large n.
A zero pivot stops the method; a full zero row signals no solution or infinitely many.
Always check the answer by plugging it into an original equation.
lessons.tip: Write the full augmented matrix after every single row operation. It feels slow, but it makes every slip visible and earns method marks.
lessons.task: Solve x + y + z = 6, 2x + 3y + z = 11, x + y + 2z = 9 by Gauss elimination on paper. Then check your answer by putting it into all three equations.

quiz.q: What does forward elimination produce?
quiz.explain: All numbers below the main diagonal become zero, so the matrix is upper triangular, ready for back substitution.

quiz.q: About how many operations does Gauss elimination need for n unknowns?
quiz.explain: The three nested loops of forward elimination give roughly (2/3) n^3 floating point operations.

quiz.q: To clear a[2][1] = -3 using pivot a[1][1] = 2, the multiplier is:
quiz.explain: m = (number to clear) / pivot = -3 / 2 = -1.5.

quiz.q: Why is Cramer's rule with cofactor determinants not used for big systems?
options: Its work grows like n factorial
quiz.explain: Cofactor expansion makes the work grow like n!, which is astronomically large even for n = 20.

quiz.q: After elimination, a row reads 0 0 0 | 5. What does it mean?
quiz.explain: It says 0 = 5, which is impossible, so the equations contradict each other and there is no solution.

lessons.title: Pivoting and Ill-Conditioning
lessons.content:
Imagine you are carrying a full glass of water across a crowded room. If you walk carefully, a tiny wobble spills a drop. If you sprint, the same tiny wobble spills half the glass. In Gauss elimination, dividing by a very small pivot is like sprinting: every tiny round-off wobble gets blown up. In the last lesson we learned elimination on paper with exact numbers. Now we ask what happens on a real computer, where every number has limited digits. The answers are two ideas every engineer must know: pivoting, which fixes a bad method, and ill-conditioning, which warns you about a bad problem.

The first problem, a zero pivot: Look at the system 0x + y = 1 and x + y = 2. The answer is clearly x = 1, y = 1. But plain Gauss elimination uses the first equation's x coefficient as the pivot, and that is 0. The multiplier would be 1 / 0, so the method crashes on step one. Yet nothing is wrong with the problem. Simply writing the equations in the other order, x + y = 2 first, makes elimination work perfectly. So the order of rows matters to the method, even though it does not matter to the answer.

The sneaky problem, a tiny pivot: Now change the 0 to 0.0001. The system is 0.0001x + y = 1 and x + y = 2. The true answer is about x = 1.0001 and y = 0.9999. To see the danger clearly, pretend our computer keeps only 3 significant digits, like a cheap calculator. Real computers keep about 16 digits in double precision, but the same thing happens with bigger systems and smaller pivots, just less visibly.

Worked example without pivoting: The pivot is 0.0001, so the multiplier for row 2 is 1 / 0.0001 = 10,000. Row 2 becomes (1 - 10,000) y = 2 - 10,000, which is -9,999y = -9,998. With 3 digits, -9,999 rounds to -10,000 and -9,998 also rounds to -10,000. So y = 1. Back substitution: 0.0001x = 1 - y = 0, so x = 0. The true x is about 1. We got 0. A 100 percent error, from one tiny pivot.

Why it went so wrong: The huge multiplier 10,000 swamped the original numbers 1 and 2 in row 2; they became invisible next to 10,000 after rounding. That information was lost forever. Then in back substitution, the small error in y was divided by the tiny 0.0001, which multiplies it by 10,000. Tiny pivot means huge multiplier on the way down and huge division on the way up. Both blow up round-off.

Worked example with pivoting: Swap the rows first so the bigger number becomes the pivot: x + y = 2 on top, 0.0001x + y = 1 below. The multiplier is now 0.0001 / 1 = 0.0001. Row 2 becomes (1 - 0.0001) y = 1 - 0.0002, which is 0.9999y = 0.9998. With 3 digits, both round to 1.00, so y = 1. Then x = 2 - y = 1. The answer x = 1, y = 1 is correct to 3 digits. Same computer, same rounding, totally different quality. The only change was the row order.

Partial pivoting, the rule: Before eliminating column k, look at all the entries in column k from row k down to the bottom. Pick the one with the largest absolute value, and swap its row up into position k. Then eliminate as usual. Because the pivot is the biggest in its column, every multiplier has absolute value at most 1. Multipliers no bigger than 1 cannot blow up the other numbers, which keeps round-off under control. That is the whole trick, and it costs only some comparisons and row swaps, tiny compared with the n^3 arithmetic.

Partial pivoting on a 3 by 3: Take rows (1, 2, 3 | 14), (4, 5, 6 | 32), (7, 8, 10 | 53). Column 1 entries are 1, 4 and 7, so 7 is the biggest. Swap rows 1 and 3, giving (7, 8, 10 | 53) on top. Multipliers become 4/7 and 1/7, both less than 1. After eliminating, look at column 2 in rows 2 and 3, pick the larger in absolute value, swap if needed, and continue. The answer, x = 1, y = 2, z = 3, comes out the same as without pivoting in exact arithmetic, but with much less round-off in floating point.

Inside the computer: Swapping rows in a big matrix sounds expensive, but libraries usually keep a small permutation array, like p = [3, 2, 1], that remembers which original row sits where. Swapping two entries of p is instant. This record is also needed later: in LU decomposition, the swaps become a permutation matrix P, giving PA = LU.

Complete pivoting and scaling: Complete pivoting searches the whole remaining sub-matrix for the largest number and swaps both rows and columns. It is a little safer but much slower to search, and column swaps reorder the unknowns, so it is rarely used. Scaled partial pivoting handles another trap: if one equation is written with huge numbers, like 2x + 300,000y = 300,000, its x coefficient 2 is not really big compared with the rest of its row. Scaled pivoting compares each candidate divided by the largest number in its own row, so a row is not chosen just because someone wrote it in larger units.

The second idea, ill-conditioning: Pivoting fixes a weak method. But some problems are fragile by nature, no matter how good the method is. Look at x + y = 2 and x + 1.0001y = 2.0001. The answer is x = 1, y = 1. Now change the last number by a tiny 0.0001, to 2.0002. The new answer is x = 0, y = 2. A change in the fourth decimal place moved the answer by a whole unit. Such a system is called ill-conditioned.

Why ill-conditioning happens: Picture the two equations as straight lines. Their slopes are almost the same, so the lines are nearly parallel and cross at a very thin angle. Shift one line by a hair and the crossing point slides far along the other line. Well-conditioned systems are like two lines crossing at a sharp angle, close to a plus sign; nudging one barely moves the crossing.

Condition number: Mathematicians measure this fragility with the condition number of A, written cond(A). Roughly, it tells you how much a small relative change in the data can be magnified in the answer. If cond(A) is about 10^k, you may lose about k digits of accuracy. Our nearly parallel example has cond(A) of about 40,000, so you can lose about 4 or 5 digits. With double precision's roughly 16 digits, you would still trust about 11. A well-conditioned identity-like matrix has cond(A) near 1. A singular matrix has infinite condition number.

How the condition number is computed: The formula is cond(A) = ||A|| times ||A inverse||, where ||A|| is a norm, a single number that measures how much the matrix can stretch a vector. A matrix that stretches some directions a lot and squashes others almost to nothing has a big condition number, because its inverse must then stretch those squashed directions back hugely. Computing the inverse just to get this number would be wasteful, so libraries estimate it cheaply as a side product of elimination. MATLAB, for example, prints a warning that the matrix is close to singular or badly scaled when the estimate is very large. Treat that warning seriously: it means the digits you see may be partly noise.

Residual versus error: A tempting way to check an answer is the residual r = b - A times x_computed. If the residual is tiny, surely the answer is right? Not for ill-conditioned systems. Take the wrong answer x = 0, y = 2 for the original system: x + y = 2 is exact, and x + 1.0001y = 2.0002, only 0.0001 off from 2.0001. The residual is tiny, yet each unknown is wrong by 1. A small residual only proves a small error when the system is well-conditioned.

Real-life example 1, a factory in Gazipur: Engineers estimate how much two similar dyes contribute to a fabric's colour from two light sensor readings. If both dyes absorb nearly the same colours, the two equations are almost the same line, so the system is ill-conditioned. A tiny sensor error, like dust on the lens, can make the computed amounts wildly wrong, even negative. The fix is not a better solver but better data: measure at a wavelength where the dyes differ more.

Real-life example 2, GPS position: Your phone finds its position by solving equations from several satellites. If all the visible satellites happen to be bunched in one small part of the sky, the equations become nearly dependent, and the position error grows. GPS engineers call this geometric dilution of precision. It is ill-conditioning in action, and it is why your location jumps around in narrow lanes of Old Dhaka where tall buildings hide much of the sky.

When to use pivoting: Practically always. Every serious library solver, such as LAPACK, which sits under MATLAB, NumPy and many others, uses partial pivoting by default for general matrices. The cost is tiny and the safety is big. You can skip it for special matrices known to be safe, like strictly diagonally dominant or symmetric positive definite ones, where the natural pivots are already big enough.

When pivoting does not help: Pivoting cannot rescue an ill-conditioned problem. If the lines are nearly parallel, the problem itself amplifies data errors; the best method can only avoid adding more error of its own. Then you need better data, more digits, or a reformulated problem.

Common mistakes: First, pivoting by the largest number in the row instead of in the column below the pivot. Second, forgetting to swap the right-hand side b along with the row. Third, believing a small residual means a correct answer. Fourth, blaming the method for an ill-conditioned problem, or the problem for a missing pivot step. Fifth, thinking more digits fix everything: they help with round-off, but they cannot remove errors already in measured data.

What exams ask: "Solve this system with and without partial pivoting using 3 or 4 significant digits and compare", "What is partial pivoting and why does it reduce round-off?", "Define an ill-conditioned system with an example", "What does the condition number tell you?", and "Why can a small residual be misleading?". Show the rounding at each step; that is where marks are.

Mental model: Two separate dials. Dial one is the method: without pivoting it may wobble even on a calm problem, and pivoting steadies it. Dial two is the problem: its condition number says how much the problem itself shakes when the data shakes. A good answer needs both dials in a safe position.

Recap: Tiny pivots create huge multipliers that magnify round-off. Partial pivoting picks the largest absolute value in the column as the pivot, keeping multipliers at most 1. Ill-conditioned systems, like nearly parallel lines, magnify small data errors no matter the method; the condition number measures how badly, and a small residual does not guarantee a small error.
key_points: A zero pivot stops Gauss elimination; a tiny pivot silently destroys accuracy through huge multipliers.
Partial pivoting swaps up the row with the largest absolute value in the current column, so every multiplier is at most 1 in size.
With 3-digit arithmetic, 0.0001x + y = 1, x + y = 2 gives x = 0 without pivoting and x = 1 with pivoting.
Scaled partial pivoting compares candidates relative to the largest number in their own row.
An ill-conditioned system changes its answer a lot when the data changes a little, like nearly parallel lines.
If cond(A) is about 10^k, expect to lose about k digits of accuracy.
A small residual guarantees a small error only for well-conditioned systems.
Pivoting fixes the method; it cannot fix an ill-conditioned problem.
lessons.tip: When an exam asks for limited significant digits, round after every single operation, not just at the end. That rounding is exactly what makes the pivoting difference visible.
lessons.task: Using a calculator and rounding every result to 3 significant digits, solve 0.00001x + y = 1, x + y = 2 first without and then with row swapping. Compare both answers with the true answer near x = 1.00001, y = 0.99999.

quiz.q: In partial pivoting, which entry becomes the pivot for column k?
options: The largest absolute value in column k from row k downward
The largest number in row k
The smallest non-zero entry in column k
quiz.explain: We search the column below and including the diagonal and swap up the largest absolute value.

quiz.q: Why does partial pivoting reduce round-off error?
options: It keeps every multiplier at most 1 in absolute value
It reduces the number of unknowns
quiz.explain: With the biggest pivot in the column, every multiplier has size at most 1, so it cannot blow up other numbers.

quiz.q: Changing b from 2.0001 to 2.0002 changes the answer from (1, 1) to (0, 2). The system is:
quiz.explain: A tiny change in data giving a huge change in the answer is the definition of ill-conditioning.

quiz.q: If cond(A) is about 10^6 and you work with about 16 digits, roughly how many correct digits can you trust?
quiz.explain: You may lose about 6 digits, leaving roughly 16 - 6 = 10.

quiz.q: A computed answer has a tiny residual. What can you conclude?
options: It is accurate only if the system is well-conditioned
quiz.explain: For ill-conditioned systems, a wrong answer can still have a tiny residual.

lessons.title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and the Matrix Inverse
lessons.content:
Imagine two ways to tidy a messy room. In the first way, you push everything into neat piles on one side and then, later, pick items out of the piles one by one when you need them. In the second way, you put every single item straight into its final drawer, so when you are done, anything can be grabbed instantly. Gauss elimination is the first way: it leaves a triangle and finishes with back substitution. Gauss-Jordan elimination is the second way: it keeps cleaning until each unknown sits alone in its own row, and the answer can be read off directly. In this lesson we learn Gauss-Jordan, use it to find a matrix inverse, and, just as important, learn when not to.

A little history: Elimination is old. A Chinese book, The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, written about two thousand years ago, already solved grain and price problems by arranging numbers on a counting board and eliminating column by column. Gauss used elimination around 1800 to compute the orbits of asteroids from telescope data. The extra cleaning step is linked to Wilhelm Jordan, a German surveyor who described it in 1888 in a book on measuring land, where people had to solve many small systems by hand and liked reading the answer straight off the page.

The goal, reduced row echelon form: Gauss elimination stops when the matrix is upper triangular, with zeros only below the diagonal. Gauss-Jordan goes further. It makes every pivot equal to 1 and also makes zeros above each pivot. For a square system with a unique answer, the left side of the augmented matrix becomes the identity matrix I, with ones on the diagonal and zeros everywhere else. Then the right column is the answer itself: row 1 says x = something, row 2 says y = something, and so on. This final shape is called reduced row echelon form.

The rule in plain words: For each column k, from left to right: first, divide the pivot row by the pivot, so the pivot becomes 1. Second, for every other row i, above and below, subtract (that row's entry in column k) times the pivot row. Since the pivot is now 1, the multiplier is simply the entry you want to remove. After processing all columns, the left part is I.

Worked example, setting up: Solve x + y + z = 6, 2y + 5z = -4, 2x + 5y - z = 27. The augmented matrix has rows (1, 1, 1 | 6), (0, 2, 5 | -4), (2, 5, -1 | 27).

Column 1: The pivot is already 1. Row 2 already has 0 in column 1. Row 3 has 2, so row 3 minus 2 times row 1: (2 - 2, 5 - 2, -1 - 2 | 27 - 12) = (0, 3, -3 | 15). Now column 1 is (1, 0, 0), exactly like the first column of I.

Column 2: The pivot is 2 in row 2. Divide row 2 by 2: (0, 1, 2.5 | -2). Now clear above and below. Row 1 minus 1 times row 2: (1, 0, -1.5 | 8). Row 3 minus 3 times row 2: (0, 0, -3 - 7.5 | 15 + 6) = (0, 0, -10.5 | 21). Notice the difference from plain Gauss elimination: we also cleaned row 1, above the pivot.

Column 3: The pivot is -10.5. Divide row 3 by -10.5: (0, 0, 1 | -2). Clear above. Row 1 minus (-1.5) times row 3, meaning plus 1.5 times row 3: (1, 0, 0 | 8 - 3) = (1, 0, 0 | 5). Row 2 minus 2.5 times row 3: (0, 1, 0 | -2 + 5) = (0, 1, 0 | 3). The matrix reads (1, 0, 0 | 5), (0, 1, 0 | 3), (0, 0, 1 | -2). So x = 5, y = 3, z = -2, with no back substitution needed. Check: 2(5) + 5(3) - (-2) = 10 + 15 + 2 = 27. Correct.

What the inverse is: For numbers, the inverse of 4 is 1/4, because 4 times 1/4 = 1. For a square matrix A, the inverse A^-1 is the matrix with A times A^-1 = I. If you know A^-1, then the solution of Ax = b is x = A^-1 b, because multiplying both sides by A^-1 leaves x alone. Only non-singular matrices, with a non-zero determinant, have inverses. A singular matrix, like one with two equal rows, squashes some information flat, and nothing can unsquash it.

Why the [A | I] trick works: Think of solving Ax = e1, Ax = e2 and Ax = e3 at the same time, where e1, e2, e3 are the columns of I. Their three solutions are exactly the three columns of A^-1. Gauss-Jordan can carry many right-hand sides together, so we glue all of I next to A, forming [A | I], and row-reduce. When the left side becomes I, the right side has become A^-1. Another way to see it: every row operation is the same as multiplying on the left by some matrix. If all of them together turn A into I, their combined product is A^-1, and applying the same operations to I writes that product down.

Small inverse example: Take A with rows (2, 1) and (1, 1). Start with (2, 1 | 1, 0) and (1, 1 | 0, 1). Divide row 1 by 2: (1, 0.5 | 0.5, 0). Row 2 minus row 1: (0, 0.5 | -0.5, 1). Multiply row 2 by 2: (0, 1 | -1, 2). Row 1 minus 0.5 times row 2: (1, 0 | 1, -1). So A^-1 has rows (1, -1) and (-1, 2). Check one entry of A times A^-1: row 1 of A, (2, 1), times column 1 of A^-1, (1, -1), gives 2 - 1 = 1. Good.

A 3 by 3 inverse: Take A with rows (1, 0, 2), (2, -1, 3), (4, 1, 8). Row-reducing [A | I] in the same way, column by column, ends with A^-1 having rows (-11, 2, 2), (-4, 0, 1), (6, -1, -1). Check the first row of A times the first column of A^-1: 1(-11) + 0(-4) + 2(6) = -11 + 12 = 1. And the first row of A times the second column: 1(2) + 0(0) + 2(-1) = 0. Each check that gives 1 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere confirms the inverse.

What happens inside the computer: Gauss-Jordan uses the same nested loops as Gauss elimination, but the inner loop over rows runs over all rows except the pivot row, not only the rows below. That one change is why it does more work. Partial pivoting is still used, exactly as in the last lesson: before scaling, swap up the row with the largest absolute value in the column.

How much work: For one right-hand side, Gauss-Jordan needs about n^3 operations, compared with about (2/3) n^3 for Gauss elimination plus a cheap n^2 back substitution. So Gauss-Jordan is roughly 50 percent more expensive for solving. Computing a full inverse costs about 2n^3. Then multiplying A^-1 by b costs another n^2. For n = 1,000, solving directly costs about 0.67 billion operations, while forming the inverse costs about 2 billion. On top of being slower, the inverse route usually adds a little more round-off error.

When the inverse is actually needed: Sometimes you really want the matrix A^-1 itself, not just one solution. In statistics, the inverse of a certain matrix gives the variances of fitted coefficients, so you can say how sure you are about each one. In small 2 by 2 or 3 by 3 geometry problems, like rotating and un-rotating points in a game, a ready-made inverse is handy and cheap. In theory and proofs, writing x = A^-1 b is a clean way to talk, even if the computer never forms A^-1.

When not to compute the inverse: If your goal is to solve Ax = b, even for many different b vectors, do not invert. Factor A once with LU decomposition, which you will see in the next lesson, and reuse the factors for each new b at only about n^2 cost each. Numerical analysts have a famous rule: you almost never need to compute an inverse. If you see inv(A) * b in code, it is usually a sign that a solver call would be faster and more accurate.

Real-life example 1, a university results office: Suppose an office in Rajshahi must convert raw scores using the same fixed 3 by 3 scaling system for thousands of students, each with a different right-hand side. A beginner might compute A^-1 once and multiply. That works for a 3 by 3 matrix, since the cost is tiny either way. But if the system were 5,000 by 5,000, the LU route would be both faster and more accurate. Knowing the size where habits start to matter is real engineering judgment.

Real-life example 2, a mobile game camera: A game made by a team in Dhaka moves a camera around a 3D world. Each frame, the camera's position and rotation form a small 4 by 4 matrix, and the game needs its inverse to turn world coordinates into what the camera sees. Here the inverse truly is the object needed, the matrix is tiny, and for rotation-plus-shift matrices there is even a quick shortcut: the inverse of a pure rotation is just its transpose. So the inverse is the right tool in this case.

Gauss versus Gauss-Jordan side by side: Gauss elimination makes zeros only below each pivot and then back-substitutes, costing about (2/3) n^3. Gauss-Jordan makes zeros above and below and scales pivots to 1, costing about n^3, and needs no back substitution. Gauss is the better choice for solving. Gauss-Jordan is easier to read on paper and is the natural way to compute an inverse or the reduced echelon form used to study rank and free variables.
