Common mistakes: First, forgetting to clear entries above the pivot, which turns Gauss-Jordan back into Gauss elimination. Second, scaling the pivot row but not its right-hand side, or not the I part. Third, using an old version of the pivot row after it was already scaled. Fourth, trying to invert a singular matrix: you will hit a column with no non-zero pivot available; that is the method telling you no inverse exists. Fifth, solving with the inverse when a plain solve was enough.

What exams ask: "Solve this system by Gauss-Jordan elimination", "Find the inverse of this 3 by 3 matrix by row reduction", "Compare the operation counts of Gauss and Gauss-Jordan", "Why is computing the inverse not recommended for solving systems?", and "What is reduced row echelon form?". For inverse questions, always finish by checking at least one row times column of A A^-1.

Mental model: Gauss elimination builds a staircase and then walks back up it. Gauss-Jordan tears the staircase down completely until each unknown stands alone on its own floor, which is cleaner to look at but costs more effort. The [A | I] trick is just Gauss-Jordan carrying several right-hand sides at once.

Recap: Gauss-Jordan makes each pivot 1 and clears both above and below, ending with the identity matrix and the answer in the last column. Row-reducing [A | I] produces A^-1. It costs about n^3 for a solve and 2n^3 for an inverse, more than Gauss elimination, so for solving systems we prefer elimination or LU, and we form an inverse only when the inverse itself is what we need.
key_points: Gauss-Jordan makes every pivot 1 and clears entries both above and below it, giving reduced row echelon form.
For a square non-singular system the left side becomes I and the last column is the answer, with no back substitution.
Row-reducing [A | I] until the left side is I turns the right side into A^-1.
Only non-singular matrices (non-zero determinant) have an inverse.
Gauss-Jordan costs about n^3 per solve versus about (2/3) n^3 for Gauss elimination; a full inverse costs about 2n^3.
To solve Ax = b, even for many b, factor with LU instead of computing the inverse.
Compute an inverse only when the inverse itself is needed, such as small geometry transforms or variance formulas.
lessons.tip: After finding an inverse, multiply one row of A by every column of your answer. You should get one 1 and the rest zeros. It is the fastest way to catch an arithmetic slip.
lessons.task: Find the inverse of the matrix with rows (3, 2) and (1, 1) by row-reducing [A | I] on paper. Then multiply A by your answer and confirm you get the identity matrix.

quiz.q: What does Gauss-Jordan do that Gauss elimination does not?
options: Clears entries above each pivot too
quiz.explain: Gauss elimination only clears below the pivot; Gauss-Jordan clears above and below and scales pivots to 1.

quiz.q: When [A | I] is fully row-reduced to [I | B], what is B?
quiz.explain: The same row operations that turn A into I turn I into A^-1.

quiz.q: The inverse of the matrix with rows (2, 1) and (1, 1) has rows:
quiz.explain: Row reduction gives (1, -1), (-1, 2), and A times it gives I.

quiz.q: Roughly how does the cost of Gauss-Jordan for one solve compare with Gauss elimination?
quiz.explain: Clearing above the pivots too makes Gauss-Jordan about 50 percent more expensive.

quiz.q: You need to solve Ax = b for 500 different b vectors with the same large A. What is best?
options: Factor A once (LU) and reuse it for each b
quiz.explain: LU factors once at about (2/3) n^3, then each new b costs only about n^2, and it is more accurate than using the inverse.

lessons.title: LU Decomposition
lessons.content:
Imagine a tailor in Dhaka's New Market who makes school uniforms. The slow part is measuring each student and cutting a paper pattern. Sewing the cloth is quick. If the same student comes back for five more shirts in different colours, a smart tailor does not measure again. He keeps the pattern and just cuts new cloth. LU decomposition is that saved pattern for linear systems. The slow part of solving Ax = b is the elimination work on A. If A stays the same and only b changes, we should do that heavy work once, save it, and reuse it. This lesson shows how.

The problem LU solves: From lesson 11, Gauss elimination costs about (2/3) n^3 operations, and almost all of that is spent turning A into a triangle. The right-hand side b only goes along for the ride. Now think of real jobs: an engineer tests one bridge design under 200 different truck loads, so A, the structure, is fixed and b, the load, changes 200 times. A circuit simulator steps through time, and at each step the same circuit matrix meets a new b. Repeating full elimination every time throws away the same work again and again.

What LU means: LU decomposition writes the square matrix A as a product A = LU. L is lower triangular, with numbers only on and below the diagonal, and U is upper triangular, with numbers only on and above the diagonal. In the most common version, called Doolittle's method, L has ones on its diagonal. The surprising part is that you already know how to get L and U: U is the triangle that Gauss elimination produces, and L simply stores the multipliers you used along the way.

Why triangles are good: Solving with a triangular matrix is cheap and easy. With an upper triangle, the last equation has one unknown, so you do back substitution, as in lesson 11. With a lower triangle, the first equation has one unknown, so you do forward substitution, going from the top down. Each takes only about n^2 operations, much less than n^3.

How to solve with LU: Since Ax = b and A = LU, we have L(Ux) = b. Call the unknown vector Ux by a new name, y. Then solving is two easy steps. Step 1: solve Ly = b by forward substitution to get y. Step 2: solve Ux = y by back substitution to get x. That is it. Two cheap triangle solves replace one expensive elimination.

Worked example, finding L and U: Take A with rows (2, 1, 1), (4, 3, 3), (8, 7, 9). Column 1: the pivot is 2. The multiplier for row 2 is 4 / 2 = 2, and row 2 minus 2 times row 1 gives (0, 1, 1). The multiplier for row 3 is 8 / 2 = 4, and row 3 minus 4 times row 1 gives (0, 3, 5). Column 2: the pivot is 1. The multiplier for row 3 is 3 / 1 = 3, and row 3 minus 3 times row 2 gives (0, 0, 2). So U has rows (2, 1, 1), (0, 1, 1), (0, 0, 2).

Placing the multipliers: Put each multiplier into L at the same position as the number it destroyed. m21 = 2 goes to row 2, column 1. m31 = 4 goes to row 3, column 1. m32 = 3 goes to row 3, column 2. Ones go on the diagonal. So L has rows (1, 0, 0), (2, 1, 0), (4, 3, 1). Check one entry of L times U: row 3 of L, (4, 3, 1), times column 3 of U, (1, 1, 2), gives 4 + 3 + 2 = 9, the original a33. Multiply everything out and you get A back exactly.

Why the multipliers land in L: Each elimination step, row i minus m times row k, can be undone by adding m times row k back. Undoing all steps in reverse order rebuilds A from U, and the matrix doing that rebuilding is exactly L with the multipliers sitting where they were used. So L is the record of how to get from U back to A.

Worked example, first right-hand side: Let b = (4, 10, 24). Forward substitution on Ly = b: y1 = 4. Row 2 says 2y1 + y2 = 10, so y2 = 10 - 8 = 2. Row 3 says 4y1 + 3y2 + y3 = 24, so y3 = 24 - 16 - 6 = 2. So y = (4, 2, 2). Back substitution on Ux = y: 2z = 2, so z = 1. y + z = 2, so y = 1. 2x + y + z = 4, so 2x = 2 and x = 1. The answer is x = (1, 1, 1).

Worked example, a second right-hand side: Now b = (1, 1, 1). We do not touch A again. Forward: y1 = 1, y2 = 1 - 2 = -1, y3 = 1 - 4(1) - 3(-1) = 1 - 4 + 3 = 0. Back: 2z = 0 so z = 0; y + 0 = -1 so y = -1; 2x - 1 + 0 = 1 so x = 1. The answer is (1, -1, 0). Check in the original: 4(1) + 3(-1) + 3(0) = 1. Correct. The second solve took only a handful of operations.

The cost picture: Factoring A costs about (2/3) n^3, the same as one elimination. Each later solve costs about 2n^2, forward plus back. For n = 1,000 and 100 right-hand sides, redoing elimination each time would cost about 100 times 0.67 billion, around 67 billion operations. LU costs 0.67 billion once plus 100 times about 2 million, around 0.87 billion in total. That is almost 80 times less work.

Determinant for free: The determinant of a product is the product of determinants, and the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal. L has ones on its diagonal, so det(L) = 1. Therefore det(A) = det(U) = the product of the pivots. In our example, det(A) = 2 times 1 times 2 = 4. This is how computers actually compute determinants: never by cofactor expansion, always by elimination.

Pivoting inside LU: Real solvers use partial pivoting, as in lesson 12, so they produce PA = LU, where P is a permutation matrix that records the row swaps. To solve, first reorder b with the same swaps, then do the two triangle solves as usual. Each row swap flips the sign of the determinant, so det(A) equals the product of pivots times plus or minus 1, depending on whether the number of swaps is even or odd.

When plain LU does not exist: Take the matrix with rows (0, 1) and (1, 1). It is perfectly invertible, since its determinant is -1, but the very first pivot is 0, so no multiplier can be formed and no L and U exist in the plain form. Swap the two rows and the problem disappears: the swapped matrix has L with rows (1, 0), (0, 1) and U equal to itself. This is a key fact: every invertible matrix has a PA = LU factorisation, but not every one has A = LU without the P.

Inside the computer: Libraries store L and U inside the original array to save memory. The upper part, including the diagonal, holds U. The lower part, below the diagonal, holds the multipliers of L; its ones are not stored because everyone knows they are there. So LU needs no more memory than A itself. In Python, scipy.linalg.lu_factor returns this packed matrix plus the pivot array, and lu_solve reuses it for any new b.

Other versions, Crout and Cholesky: Crout's method is the same idea but puts the ones on the diagonal of U instead of L. Cholesky decomposition is a special shortcut for matrices that are symmetric (a_ij = a_ji) and positive definite, which appear a lot in physics and statistics. It writes A = L L^T, with only one triangle to find, and costs about half of LU, about (1/3) n^3. For example, the matrix with rows (4, 2) and (2, 3) has L with rows (2, 0) and (1, square root of 2), because 2 times 2 = 4, 1 times 2 = 2, and 1 + 2 = 3.

Real-life example 1, bridge loads: An engineering firm checks a new bridge over the Padma river region under many traffic patterns: one truck on the left, three buses in the middle, a crowd on a festival day. The stiffness matrix A describes the bridge and does not change. Each traffic pattern is a new load vector b. The software factors A once, then solves for every pattern in a fraction of the time. Same pattern, many shirts.

Real-life example 2, a circuit through time: Simulating a phone charger circuit over a millisecond may take thousands of time steps. For simple linear circuits with a fixed step size, the matrix stays the same at each step while the sources change, so one LU factorisation serves the whole run. When the circuit has nonlinear parts like diodes, the matrix changes and must be refactored, which is one reason those simulations are slower.

When to use LU: Use it whenever you will solve with the same A more than once, need the determinant, or want a dependable direct method for dense systems up to a few thousand unknowns. It is what most library "solve" functions do inside, even when you call them only once.

When not to use it: If A changes every time, LU gives no reuse advantage over plain elimination. For huge sparse systems, LU fills in many zeros, called fill-in, and can run out of memory; iterative methods from the next lesson, or special sparse LU with clever row orderings, are used instead. And if A is symmetric positive definite, use Cholesky instead, since it is twice as fast.

Common mistakes: First, putting the multipliers in L with the wrong sign; Doolittle stores m itself, not minus m, when you compute row i minus m times row k. Second, forgetting the ones on L's diagonal. Third, solving Ux = b directly and forgetting the forward step with L. Fourth, ignoring the permutation P when pivoting was used. Fifth, doing a full refactorisation for each new b, which defeats the whole point.

What exams ask: "Decompose this 3 by 3 matrix into LU by Doolittle's method and solve Ax = b", "Why is LU preferred when many right-hand sides share the same A?", "Find the determinant from the LU factors", "State the difference between Doolittle, Crout and Cholesky", and "What is the cost of factoring and of each solve?". Always verify by multiplying at least one row of L by one column of U.

Mental model: LU is elimination with a memory. Gauss elimination does the work and throws away the multipliers; LU keeps them in L. U is the staircase, L is the instruction sheet for building it. Then any new b just walks down L and back up U.

Recap: A = LU, with U from elimination and L holding the multipliers with ones on its diagonal. Solve Ly = b forwards and then Ux = y backwards. Factoring costs about (2/3) n^3 once, and each new right-hand side only about 2n^2. The determinant is the product of U's diagonal, with a sign flip per row swap. Cholesky does the job in half the time for symmetric positive definite matrices.
key_points: LU decomposition writes A = LU with L lower triangular and U upper triangular.
In Doolittle's method U comes from Gauss elimination and L stores the multipliers, with ones on its diagonal.
Solve Ax = b in two cheap steps: Ly = b forwards, then Ux = y backwards.
Factoring costs about (2/3) n^3 once; each new right-hand side costs only about 2n^2.
det(A) is the product of U's diagonal, with a sign change for each row swap.
With pivoting the factorisation is PA = LU, and b must be reordered by P first.
Crout puts the ones on U's diagonal; Cholesky (A = L L^T) is for symmetric positive definite matrices and costs about half.
lessons.tip: Write L and U side by side as you eliminate: each time you compute a multiplier, drop it straight into L at the position you just zeroed. Then you never have to redo the elimination.
lessons.task: Find the Doolittle LU decomposition of the matrix with rows (1, 2) and (3, 8). Use it to solve Ax = b for b = (5, 19) and then for b = (1, 1). Check both answers in the original equations.

quiz.q: In Doolittle's LU decomposition, what does L contain below its diagonal?
quiz.explain: Each multiplier m_ik is stored in L at the position it zeroed, with ones on the diagonal.

quiz.q: To solve Ax = b with A = LU, what is the correct order?
options: Solve Ux = b, then Ly = x
Invert L and U, then multiply
Solve Ly = b forwards, then Ux = y backwards
Solve Ux = y forwards, then Ly = b backwards
quiz.explain: Since L(Ux) = b, first find y = Ux from Ly = b, then find x from Ux = y.

quiz.q: If U has diagonal entries 2, 1 and 2 and no row swaps were made, what is det(A)?
quiz.explain: det(A) = det(L) det(U) = 1 times (2 times 1 times 2) = 4.

quiz.q: Why is LU especially useful for many right-hand sides with the same A?
options: It works only for symmetric matrices
The (2/3) n^3 factoring is done once and each new b costs only about 2n^2
quiz.explain: The heavy work is reused, so each extra solve is cheap.

quiz.q: Cholesky decomposition A = L L^T can be used when A is:
quiz.explain: Cholesky needs a symmetric positive definite matrix and costs about half of LU.

lessons.title: Iterative Methods: Gauss-Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel
lessons.content:
Imagine a group of friends trying to split a restaurant bill fairly, but nobody knows exactly what everyone ate. Each person makes a guess about their own share based on what the others currently think they owe. Then everybody updates, again using the latest guesses of the others. After a few rounds, the guesses stop changing much, and the bill is settled. Nobody solved a big equation; they just kept improving guesses. That is the spirit of iterative methods for linear systems. The last few lessons were direct methods: they finish in a fixed number of steps. Now we learn methods that start from a guess and improve it round after round, just like Newton-Raphson or fixed-point iteration did for a single equation.

Why we need another approach: Direct methods like Gauss elimination and LU cost about (2/3) n^3 operations and need the whole matrix in memory. Now think of a flood model of the Bangladesh delta split into a grid of one million cells. Each cell's water level depends only on its few neighbours, so each equation has maybe five non-zero numbers out of a million. Such a matrix is called sparse. Elimination would fill in many of those zeros, needing far more memory than the computer has, and the n^3 time would be astronomical. Iterative methods only ever touch the non-zero entries, so they fit these problems naturally.

The basic idea: Take equation 1 and solve it for x1 in terms of the other unknowns. Take equation 2 and solve it for x2, and so on. Now you have formulas like x1 = (b1 - other terms) / a11. Start with any guess, often all zeros, plug the guess into the right-hand sides, and get a new guess. Repeat. If the method converges, each new guess is closer to the true answer. This is exactly fixed-point iteration from lesson 9, but for a whole vector at once.

What happens inside the computer: The program keeps the unknowns in an array x. For Jacobi it also keeps a second array x_new. In each round, a loop goes over i from 1 to n and computes x_new[i] = (b[i] - sum of a[i][j] times x[j] for every j not equal to i) / a[i][i]. After the loop, x_new is copied into x and the change is measured. For Seidel there is only one array: the loop writes x[i] directly, so later rows in the same loop automatically see the fresh values. For sparse matrices, the sum runs only over the stored non-zero entries of row i, which is what makes each round so cheap.

Our example system: Use 10x + y + z = 12, x + 10y + z = 12, x + y + 10z = 12. The true answer is x = y = z = 1, which you can check: 10 + 1 + 1 = 12. Rewritten: x = (12 - y - z) / 10, y = (12 - x - z) / 10, z = (12 - x - y) / 10.

Gauss-Jacobi method: In Jacobi, every new value in a round is computed only from the old values of the previous round. Round 1, starting from x = y = z = 0: x = 12 / 10 = 1.2, y = 1.2, z = 1.2. Round 2, using 1.2 for everything: x = (12 - 1.2 - 1.2) / 10 = 0.96, and the same for y and z. Round 3: x = (12 - 0.96 - 0.96) / 10 = 1.008. Round 4: x = (12 - 1.008 - 1.008) / 10 = 0.9984. The guesses jump above and below 1 and settle quickly toward 1.

Gauss-Seidel method: Seidel makes one smart change: as soon as a new value is computed, use it immediately in the rest of the same round. Round 1 from zeros: x = (12 - 0 - 0) / 10 = 1.2. Then y = (12 - 1.2 - 0) / 10 = 1.08, using the new x. Then z = (12 - 1.2 - 1.08) / 10 = 0.972, using the new x and y. Round 2: x = (12 - 1.08 - 0.972) / 10 = 0.9948, y = (12 - 0.9948 - 0.972) / 10 = 1.00332, z = (12 - 0.9948 - 1.00332) / 10 = 1.000188. Round 3 gives about 0.99965, 1.00002, 1.00003. After three rounds Seidel's worst error is about 0.00035, while Jacobi's after three rounds is 0.008.

Why Seidel is usually faster: Newer values are usually better values, so using them at once spreads good information faster. In many common problems, especially grid problems from physics, Gauss-Seidel needs about half as many rounds as Jacobi for the same accuracy. It also needs less memory, because each new value can overwrite the old one directly in one array, while Jacobi must keep the old and new vectors separately.

Why Jacobi still matters: In Jacobi, all the new values in a round are independent of each other, since they only use the old vector. So a computer with thousands of cores, like a graphics card, can compute them all at the same time. Seidel is naturally sequential: y must wait for the new x. On parallel hardware, Jacobi or a coloured variant of Seidel can win in real time even though it needs more rounds.

When does it converge? Not always: Try x + 3y = 5 and 3x + 2y = 7, whose true answer is x = 11/7, about 1.571, and y = 8/7, about 1.143. Solving equation 1 for x and equation 2 for y gives x = 5 - 3y and y = (7 - 3x) / 2. Jacobi from zeros gives (5, 3.5), then (-5.5, -4), then (17, 11.75), then (-30.25, -22). The guesses explode. The method diverges.

Diagonal dominance: A matrix is strictly diagonally dominant if, in every row, the absolute value of the diagonal number is bigger than the sum of the absolute values of all the other numbers in that row. In 10x + y + z, we have 10 > 1 + 1, so that row is dominant, and all our example rows are. If A is strictly diagonally dominant, both Jacobi and Seidel are guaranteed to converge from any starting guess. Gauss-Seidel is also guaranteed to converge when A is symmetric positive definite. These conditions are sufficient, not necessary: a method may still converge without them, but you lose the guarantee.

Fixing the bad example: In x + 3y = 5, 3x + 2y = 7, the big numbers are off the diagonal. Swap the equations: 3x + 2y = 7, x + 3y = 5. Now 3 > 2 and 3 > 1, so it is diagonally dominant. Jacobi gives x = (7 - 2y) / 3, y = (5 - x) / 3: rounds go (2.333, 1.667), (1.222, 0.889), (1.741, 1.259), (1.494, 1.086), (1.609, 1.169), creeping toward (1.571, 1.143). Seidel gets there faster: after four rounds it is at about (1.580, 1.140). Just reordering the equations changed failure into success.

Why dominance works, intuitively: Each update divides by the diagonal number. If the diagonal is big compared with the rest of the row, then an error in the other unknowns gets shrunk when it passes into the new value. Every round multiplies the error by something smaller than 1, so the error shrinks like a geometric sequence, exactly like |g'(x)| < 1 in fixed-point iteration.

When to stop: Iteration never naturally ends, so we need a stopping rule. Common choices: stop when the biggest change between two rounds is below a tolerance, such as 0.0001; or when the relative change is below a tolerance; or when the residual b - Ax is small enough. Always also set a maximum number of rounds, so a diverging run does not loop forever.

Cost per round: For a dense matrix, one round costs about n^2 operations, since each of n values uses n - 1 others. For a sparse matrix it costs only about the number of non-zero entries. If the method needs k rounds, the total is k times that. For a million-cell grid with five non-zeros per row, one round is about five million operations, and even a thousand rounds is far cheaper than elimination would ever be.

A step further, SOR: Successive over-relaxation, SOR, takes Seidel's new value and pushes a bit further in the same direction: x_new = x_old + w (x_Seidel - x_old), with a relaxation factor w between 1 and 2 for over-relaxation. With a well-chosen w, SOR can need far fewer rounds than Seidel on grid problems. With w = 1 it is just Gauss-Seidel.

Real-life example 1, flood mapping: A model of water levels across thousands of cells in a district like Sunamganj links every cell to its four neighbours. That gives a huge sparse diagonally dominant system each time step. Engineers use iterative solvers, often starting from the previous hour's water levels as the first guess, which is already very close, so only a few rounds are needed.

Real-life example 2, heat in a metal plate: A factory in Narayanganj wants the temperature at many points on a metal plate whose edges are held at known temperatures. A classic finite-difference model says each inner point's temperature is the average of its four neighbours. That is a Jacobi or Seidel update in disguise: start with any guess, keep replacing each point by the average of its neighbours, and the temperatures settle to the right pattern.

When to use iterative methods: Large sparse systems, systems where a good starting guess is available, cases where only moderate accuracy is needed, and matrices that are diagonally dominant or symmetric positive definite.

When not to use them: Small dense systems, where elimination is fast and exact in a fixed number of steps. Matrices that are not dominant and give no convergence guarantee. And many right-hand sides with the same A, where one LU factorisation may serve better.

Common mistakes: First, in Jacobi, accidentally using new values within the same round, which secretly turns it into Seidel. Second, forgetting to reorder equations to make the matrix diagonally dominant. Third, having no maximum iteration limit. Fourth, stopping after a fixed number of rounds without checking the change. Fifth, thinking divergence means a calculation error, when it often means the system was not dominant.

What exams ask: "Solve this system by Gauss-Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel to three decimal places and compare the number of iterations", "State the sufficient condition for convergence", "Why is Gauss-Seidel generally faster?", "When are iterative methods preferred over direct methods?", and "Rearrange this system so the method converges". Make a neat table with one row per iteration.

Mental model: Picture each unknown as a person who keeps adjusting their answer to agree with their neighbours. In Jacobi everyone adjusts at the same moment using the last announced answers. In Seidel each person adjusts after hearing those who just spoke. Diagonal dominance means each person trusts themselves more than all their neighbours combined, so disagreements calm down instead of growing.

Recap: Iterative methods start from a guess and improve it round after round. Jacobi uses only old values and is easy to parallelise; Seidel uses new values immediately and usually converges faster with less memory. Strict diagonal dominance guarantees convergence for both. They shine on huge sparse systems where direct methods run out of memory and time.
key_points: Iterative methods improve a starting guess round by round instead of finishing in a fixed number of steps.
Jacobi computes each new value only from the previous round's values, so all updates can run in parallel.
Seidel uses each new value immediately in the same round, usually converging faster and needing one array.
Strict diagonal dominance (|a_ii| bigger than the sum of the other |a_ij| in its row) guarantees convergence of both.
Reordering equations can turn a diverging system into a diagonally dominant, converging one.
Stop when the change or residual is below a tolerance, and always set a maximum number of rounds.
Iterative methods suit large sparse systems; direct methods suit small dense ones.
SOR pushes Seidel's update further with a factor w between 1 and 2 to speed it up.
lessons.tip: Before you iterate, check every row for diagonal dominance and swap equations if needed. Thirty seconds of checking saves a page of numbers that blow up.
lessons.task: Solve 4x + y = 9, x + 3y = 7 with Gauss-Seidel starting from x = y = 0. Do four rounds on paper, write them in a table, and compare with the exact answer you get by elimination.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between Gauss-Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel?
options: Jacobi needs pivoting and Seidel does not
Seidel uses newly computed values immediately in the same round
quiz.explain: Jacobi uses only last round's values; Seidel uses each new value as soon as it is computed.

quiz.q: Which condition guarantees that both Jacobi and Seidel converge?
options: The matrix is strictly diagonally dominant
The matrix has a zero on the diagonal
The right-hand side is all zeros
quiz.explain: If every diagonal entry beats the sum of the others in its row, both methods converge from any start.

quiz.q: For 10x + y + z = 12 etc., starting from zeros, what is Gauss-Seidel's first y value?
quiz.explain: x = 1.2 first, then y = (12 - 1.2 - 0) / 10 = 1.08 using the new x.

quiz.q: Why might Jacobi be chosen over Seidel on a graphics card?
options: All new values in a round are independent, so they can be computed in parallel
quiz.explain: Jacobi updates depend only on old values, which suits thousands of parallel cores.

quiz.q: Jacobi on x + 3y = 5, 3x + 2y = 7 blows up. What is the best first fix?
options: Swap the equations so the matrix becomes diagonally dominant
quiz.explain: After swapping, 3x + 2y = 7 and x + 3y = 5 are dominant and the iteration converges.

lessons.title: Finite Differences: Reading Patterns in a Table
lessons.content:
Imagine your uncle runs a small tea stall near Kamalapur station. Every hour he writes in a notebook how many cups he has sold since morning. He does not have a formula for his sales. He only has a table of numbers. Now he asks you: how many cups had I sold at half past ten? Or: is there a mistake somewhere in my notebook? To answer questions like these, numerical methods use a very old and very simple tool called finite differences. It works only with a table, no formula needed.

What it is: A finite difference is just the gap between two neighbouring values in a table. If the table says y = 1 at x = 1 and y = 8 at x = 2, the difference is 8 - 1 = 7. That is it. The word "finite" means the step between x values is a real, fixed size h (like 1 hour, or 0.1 metres), not an infinitely small step like in calculus. In calculus, the derivative asks "how fast does y change when x changes by a tiny amount?" A finite difference asks "how much did y change when x moved by one step h?" It is the derivative's down-to-earth cousin.

Why it exists: In real life we rarely have formulas. We have measurements: rainfall each day, the river level at Bhairab bridge every six hours, a sensor reading every second, values from a printed table of logarithms. Before computers, scientists and engineers lived on printed tables, and they needed ways to fill gaps between rows, check the tables for printing mistakes, and estimate slopes. Finite differences gave them all three. Charles Babbage even designed a machine in the 1820s called the Difference Engine, whose whole job was to build tables of polynomials using nothing but repeated addition of differences. Today the same ideas sit under interpolation (lessons 17 and 18), numerical differentiation (lesson 21) and many methods for differential equations.

The setup: We always assume equally spaced points: x0, x1 = x0 + h, x2 = x0 + 2h, and so on, with values y0, y1, y2. Equal spacing is important. Every formula in this lesson depends on it. If your points are unequally spaced, you need divided differences instead, which come in lesson 18.

Forward difference: The forward difference operator is written with the Greek capital delta, Δ. It looks ahead: Δy0 = y1 - y0, Δy1 = y2 - y1, and in general Δyk = y(k+1) - yk. The name is natural: from point k, you look forward to point k + 1. You can do it again on the differences themselves. The second forward difference is Δ²y0 = Δy1 - Δy0, which works out to y2 - 2y1 + y0. The third is Δ³y0 = y3 - 3y2 + 3y1 - y0. Notice the numbers 1, 3, 3, 1: they are binomial coefficients with alternating signs, the same numbers from Pascal's triangle. That pattern repeats for every order.

Backward difference: The backward difference operator is written ∇ and called nabla. It looks behind: ∇yk = yk - y(k-1). So ∇y1 = y1 - y0, which is exactly the same number as Δy0. The difference values in the table do not change at all. Only the label changes, depending on whether you are standing at the left end of a gap and looking forward, or standing at the right end and looking back. Why bother with two names then? Because later formulas start from the beginning of the table (they use Δ) or from the end of the table (they use ∇), and the right label makes those formulas tidy.

Central difference: The central difference operator is written δ (small delta). It sits in the middle: δy(k + 1/2) = y(k+1) - yk. The half index tells you that the difference belongs to the midpoint of the gap. Again, it is the same number in the table, just labelled as sitting between two points. Central differences are popular because a value computed in the middle is usually more balanced and more accurate, as you will see in numerical differentiation.

Building a difference table, worked: Take y = x³ at x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, so h = 1. The values are 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 343. First differences: 8 - 1 = 7, 27 - 8 = 19, then 37, 61, 91, 127. Second differences: 19 - 7 = 12, then 18, 24, 30, 36. Third differences: 18 - 12 = 6, then 6, 6, 6. Fourth differences: all 0. You write each column a little shifted, so every difference sits between the two numbers it came from. The table looks like a triangle lying on its side.

The big fact: For a polynomial of degree n, the n-th differences are constant and all higher differences are zero, as long as the spacing is equal. Why? Each time you take a difference, the degree drops by one. Take x³: (x + 1)³ - x³ = 3x² + 3x + 1, a degree 2 polynomial. Difference that again and you get a degree 1 polynomial, then a constant. The constant is exactly a × n! × hⁿ, where a is the leading coefficient. For x³ with h = 1, that is 1 × 3! × 1 = 6, which matches our table. If h were 2, the third differences of x³ would be 6 × 8 = 48.

Why the big fact is useful: It works in reverse too. If you have a table of real measurements and the third differences are nearly constant, then a cubic polynomial describes the data well, and you can safely use a cubic to fill in gaps. If the differences never settle down, a low-degree polynomial is a poor model and you should not trust interpolation far from the data. So the difference table is not only a calculation, it is a diagnostic: it tells you what kind of curve is hiding in the numbers.

Spotting a mistake in a table: Suppose someone copied the x³ table and wrote 66 instead of 64 at x = 4. That is an error of e = 2. Look at what happens. First differences: 7, 19, 39, 59, 91, 127. Second: 12, 20, 20, 32, 36. Third: 8, 0, 12, 4 instead of 6, 6, 6, 6. Subtract the correct value 6 and you get +2, -6, +6, -2. That is e times 1, -3, 3, -1, the same binomial pattern with alternating signs. So an error spreads through the table in a fan shape, growing bigger in higher columns. The middle of the fan points to the wrong entry, and the size of the pattern tells you how big the error is.

How to use that in practice: Build the table until a column should be roughly constant. Look for a place where the values jump up and down with alternating signs. Match the jumps to 1, -3, 3, -1 (for third differences) or 1, -2, 1 (for second differences). The row in the middle of the pattern is the bad entry, and the multiplier is the error. This is how old table makers caught typos in printed tables of logarithms and sines, without knowing the true values.

Effect of rounding: Real tables are rounded, say to 4 decimal places. A rounding error is at most half a unit in the last place. Because differences amplify errors with binomial coefficients, the k-th differences can carry noise up to about 2 to the power k times that rounding error. So high-order differences of rounded data quickly become noise. In practice you stop at the column where differences look roughly constant and before they start bouncing randomly. Going further does not add information, it only adds noise.

The shift operator E: Mathematicians found a neat way to write all of this. Define the shift operator E by E yk = y(k+1). It simply moves you one step to the right. Then Δ = E - 1, because Δyk = E yk - yk. Similarly ∇ = 1 - E⁻¹, since E⁻¹ moves one step left. And the central operator is δ = E^(1/2) - E^(-1/2). You can treat these operators almost like numbers. For example Δ³ = (E - 1)³ = E³ - 3E² + 3E - 1, which immediately gives Δ³y0 = y3 - 3y2 + 3y1 - y0. The binomial pattern is no longer a mystery: it is just the binomial theorem.

A taste of why E matters: Since E = 1 + Δ, moving p steps forward is E^p = (1 + Δ)^p. Expand that with the binomial series and you get y(p) = y0 + pΔy0 + p(p - 1)/2! Δ²y0 + ... That is Newton's forward interpolation formula, the star of the next lesson. So the shift operator is the bridge between "differences in a table" and "estimating values between rows". There is also a link to calculus: E = e^(hD), where D is the derivative operator, which comes from Taylor's series. That relation is what turns differences into derivative formulas later.

Real-life example 1, a shop's daily totals: A pharmacy in Mirpur records total sales at the end of each day for a week. The owner notices the second differences stay close to the same number, around 200 taka. That says sales are growing roughly like a quadratic: the daily increase itself grows by about 200 taka each day. If on Thursday the second difference suddenly jumps up and the next ones jump down in a 1, -2, 1 pattern, the owner should check Thursday's entry first. Most likely someone typed a wrong number into the register.

Real-life example 2, river level readings: The Water Development Board measures river height at fixed times. Engineers build a difference table of the readings. If the first differences are positive and the second differences are positive too, the river is not just rising, it is rising faster and faster, an early warning sign for flooding. If first differences are positive but second differences become negative, the rise is slowing down. Without any formula, the table tells the story of speed and acceleration.

When to use finite differences: Use them when your data is a table with equal spacing, when you want to check what degree of polynomial fits, when you want to hunt for copying or typing errors, and as the first step before Newton's forward or backward interpolation. They are cheap: only subtractions.

When not to use them: If the x values are unequally spaced, the simple Δ table gives wrong answers; use divided differences. If the data is very noisy (like a cheap sensor), high-order differences are mostly noise, so fitting a smooth curve by least squares (lesson 20) is wiser. And if you actually have a formula and can differentiate it by hand, you do not need a difference table to find its slope.

Common mistakes: Students mix up Δ and ∇ and think they give different numbers. They do not; only the label and where you stand differ. Another mistake is forgetting to shift columns, so a difference gets paired with the wrong row. Students also forget that the "constant n-th difference" rule needs equal spacing. In exams, a classic mistake is computing y2 - y1 for Δy2, when the correct value is y3 - y2. Write the definition at the top of your page and check it once.

What exams ask: Build a forward difference table for given data. Prove that Δ = E - 1 or that ∇ = 1 - E⁻¹. Show that the n-th difference of a degree n polynomial is constant. Find and correct one wrong entry in a table. Express Δ³y0 in terms of y values. All of these become easy once you practise building two or three tables carefully by hand.

Mental model: Picture the table as a staircase. The values are the heights of the steps. The first differences are how tall each step is. The second differences tell you whether the steps are getting taller or shorter. If at some level the change becomes perfectly even, you have found the polynomial hiding in the data. An error is like a broken step: it makes a ripple that spreads outwards with a recognisable shape.

Recap: A finite difference is the change in y over one fixed step h. Forward Δ looks ahead, backward ∇ looks behind, central δ sits in the middle, and all three use the same numbers in the table. For a degree n polynomial with equal spacing, n-th differences are constant. Errors spread with binomial coefficients and can be traced back. The shift operator E ties everything together and leads straight into Newton's interpolation formulas.
key_points: A finite difference is the change in y over one fixed step h in an equally spaced table.
Forward Δyk = y(k+1) - yk, backward ∇yk = yk - y(k-1), central δy(k+1/2) = y(k+1) - yk: same numbers, different labels.
For a degree n polynomial with equal spacing, n-th differences are constant (a × n! × hⁿ) and higher ones are zero.
A wrong entry spreads through the table with binomial coefficients like 1, -3, 3, -1, which lets you find and fix it.
Rounding noise grows in higher differences, so stop at the column that looks roughly constant.
Shift operator E yk = y(k+1); Δ = E - 1, ∇ = 1 - E⁻¹, δ = E^(1/2) - E^(-1/2).
Unequal spacing needs divided differences, not this table.
lessons.tip: Always draw the difference table with each new column shifted half a row, so every difference sits between its two parents. Most exam mistakes come from misaligned columns, not from arithmetic.
lessons.task: Write y = x² + 2x for x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and build the full difference table. Check that second differences are constant and equal 2. Then change one value by 1 on purpose and watch the 1, -2, 1 ripple appear in the second differences.

quiz.q: For y = x³ with h = 1, what are the third forward differences?
quiz.explain: For degree 3 with leading coefficient 1, the constant third difference is 3! × 1³ = 6.

quiz.q: Which relation between operators is correct?
quiz.explain: Δyk = y(k+1) - yk = E yk - yk, so Δ = E - 1. The relation 1 - E⁻¹ belongs to ∇.

quiz.q: One table entry has error e. What pattern appears in the third differences?
quiz.explain: An error spreads with binomial coefficients and alternating signs; for third differences that is 1, -3, 3, -1.

quiz.q: Δy0 and ∇y1 in the same table are:
quiz.explain: Both equal y1 - y0. Forward and backward differences use the same table values with different labels.

quiz.q: Your x values are 1, 2, 5, 9. What should you use?
options: Divided differences, because spacing is unequal
quiz.explain: Forward, backward and central difference formulas assume equal spacing h. Unequal spacing needs divided differences.

lessons.title: Newton's Forward and Backward Interpolation
lessons.content:
You come home from school at 4 pm and your mother made tea at 3:30. She measured its temperature every ten minutes from the moment she poured it: 90 degrees at 0 minutes, 75 at 10, 64 at 20 and 56 at 30. You want to know how hot it was at 5 minutes, when your little brother touched the cup and complained it was too hot. Nobody measured at 5 minutes. Interpolation is the art of estimating a value between known points in a table. Newton's forward and backward formulas are the classic way to do it when the points are equally spaced.

What interpolation is: You have a table of points (x0, y0), (x1, y1), ..., (xn, yn). You believe some smooth function f produced these values, but you do not know its formula. Interpolation finds a simple function, almost always a polynomial, that passes exactly through every point. Then you plug the in-between x into that polynomial. The polynomial is a stand-in, a substitute for the unknown f. Estimating inside the range of the table is interpolation. Estimating outside the range is extrapolation, which is much riskier.

Why polynomials: Polynomials are the easiest functions for a computer: only addition and multiplication. They can bend to fit any set of n + 1 points with distinct x values, using degree at most n. And there is a theorem (Weierstrass) that says any continuous function on a closed interval can be approximated as closely as you like by some polynomial. So polynomials are flexible, cheap and theoretically solid.

The problem before Newton: For centuries people used printed tables: logarithms, sines, star positions, tide heights. A table might give log values at 2.50 and 2.51, but you need 2.5037. The simplest fix is linear interpolation: draw a straight line between two neighbours and read off the value. That works when the table is dense and the function is nearly straight. But when the curve bends a lot, the straight line misses. Newton's idea was to add correction terms, one after another, using the difference table from lesson 16. Each correction captures more of the bending.

The variable p: Newton's formulas use equally spaced points with step h. Instead of x, we use p = (x - x0) / h. It counts how many steps x is away from x0. If x0 = 0, h = 10 and x = 5, then p = 0.5: half a step. If x = 25, then p = 2.5. Using p makes the formula the same for every table, whatever the units.

Newton's forward formula: f(x0 + ph) ≈ y0 + pΔy0 + p(p - 1)/2! Δ²y0 + p(p - 1)(p - 2)/3! Δ³y0 + ... and so on until the differences become zero or negligible. Where does it come from? From lesson 16: E = 1 + Δ, so moving p steps forward is E^p y0 = (1 + Δ)^p y0. Expand (1 + Δ)^p with the binomial series and you get exactly this. If you stop after the second term, you have linear interpolation. Every extra term bends the curve to pass through one more table point.

Why each term makes sense: The first term y0 says: start at the first value. The second term pΔy0 says: move along the first slope for p steps. The third term corrects for the slope itself changing, using the second difference. The factor p(p - 1) is zero at p = 0 and p = 1, so the correction does not disturb the first two points that the line already hits. Similarly p(p - 1)(p - 2) is zero at p = 0, 1, 2. That is the clever design: each new term fixes the next point without breaking the previous ones.

Worked example 1, a check with cubes: Take y = x³ at x = 1, 2, 3, 4: values 1, 8, 27, 64. Differences: Δy0 = 7, Δ²y0 = 12, Δ³y0 = 6. Find f(1.5). Here x0 = 1, h = 1, so p = 0.5. Compute: 1 + 0.5 × 7 + (0.5 × -0.5)/2 × 12 + (0.5 × -0.5 × -1.5)/6 × 6 = 1 + 3.5 - 1.5 + 0.375 = 3.375. And 1.5³ is exactly 3.375. It matches perfectly because the data really came from a cubic, and the formula with three differences builds a cubic.

Worked example 2, the tea: Times 0, 10, 20, 30 and temperatures 90, 75, 64, 56. First differences: -15, -11, -8. Second differences: 4, 3. Third difference: -1. We want x = 5, so p = (5 - 0)/10 = 0.5. The linear part: 90 + 0.5 × (-15) = 82.5. Add the second-difference term: 0.5 × (-0.5)/2 × 4 = -0.5, giving 82.0. Add the third: 0.5 × (-0.5) × (-1.5)/6 × (-1) = -0.0625, giving 81.9375. So the tea was about 82 degrees. Notice how the corrections shrink: -7.5, then -0.5, then -0.0625. That shrinking is the sign that the estimate is settling down and more points would barely change it.

Where forward works best: The forward formula uses y0 and the differences along the top edge of the table. Its terms are built around the first few points. So it is most accurate when x is near the start of the table, with p small, between 0 and 1. If you use it for a point at the end of a long table, p becomes large, the products p(p - 1)(p - 2) get big, and the small errors in high differences are multiplied by big numbers.

Newton's backward formula: For points near the end of the table, we flip the idea. Let xn be the last point and p = (x - xn)/h, which is negative for x inside the table. Then f(xn + ph) ≈ yn + p∇yn + p(p + 1)/2! ∇²yn + p(p + 1)(p + 2)/3! ∇³yn + ... It uses the bottom edge of the difference table: the last value and the last difference in each column. The derivation is the same trick with E⁻¹ = 1 - ∇, so E^p = (1 - ∇)^(-p).

Worked example 3, backward with cubes: Same table y = x³ at 1, 2, 3, 4. Find f(3.5). xn = 4, p = (3.5 - 4)/1 = -0.5. Backward differences at the end: ∇yn = 37, ∇²yn = 18, ∇³yn = 6. Compute: 64 + (-0.5)(37) + (-0.5)(0.5)/2 × 18 + (-0.5)(0.5)(1.5)/6 × 6 = 64 - 18.5 - 2.25 - 0.375 = 42.875. And 3.5³ = 42.875. Exact again.

Worked example 4, the tea at 25 minutes: xn = 30, p = (25 - 30)/10 = -0.5. ∇yn = -8, ∇²yn = 3, ∇³yn = -1. Linear part: 56 + (-0.5)(-8) = 60. Next: (-0.5)(0.5)/2 × 3 = -0.375, giving 59.625. Next: (-0.5)(0.5)(1.5)/6 × (-1) = +0.0625, giving 59.6875. So about 59.7 degrees.

Choosing forward or backward: Rule of thumb: near the top of the table, use forward; near the bottom, use backward; in the middle, you can use either, though central difference formulas (named after Gauss, Stirling and Bessel) are designed for the middle and usually converge faster there. All of these formulas, if you use all the points, give the same polynomial. They differ only in which terms you keep when you stop early, and in how well rounding errors behave.

How many terms: Look at your difference table. If the k-th differences are nearly constant, use terms up to Δᵏ. Adding terms beyond that mainly adds noise from rounded data. Also watch the size of each new term: once it is smaller than the accuracy you need, stop. In the tea example, the third term was only 0.06 degrees, smaller than a thermometer can measure, so you could stop at two corrections.

Inside the computer: A program for Newton's forward formula first builds the difference table, which takes about n²/2 subtractions for n + 1 points. Then it evaluates the sum, updating a running product: term = term × (p - k)/(k + 1) at each step, and adding term × Δ^(k+1)y0. That is a small loop, very cheap. If you need many x values from the same table, you build the table once and reuse it.

Real-life example 1, population between censuses: Suppose a union in Rajshahi had populations (in thousands) of 20 in 1991, 24 in 2001, 29 in 2011 and 35 in 2021. These are made-up round numbers for practice. A planner wants an estimate for 2016, near the end of the table, so backward is natural. h = 10, xn = 2021, p = -0.5. Backward differences: ∇yn = 6, ∇²yn = 1, ∇³yn = 0. Estimate: 35 + (-0.5)(6) + (-0.5)(0.5)/2 × 1 = 35 - 3 - 0.125 = 31.875, so about 31,875 people. The planner can use this to decide how many school seats or clinic beds are needed.

Real-life example 2, engineering tables: Old steam tables, tax slabs computed from formulas, or a phone's battery discharge curve measured every 10 percent all come as tables. When a charging app shows "about 37 minutes left", one simple way to produce such a number is to interpolate in a measured table instead of solving a complicated chemistry model. Real apps may use other techniques too, but the idea of reading between table rows is the same.

When to use Newton's forward or backward formula: The x values must be equally spaced. The data should be smooth and accurate (not very noisy). The x you want should lie inside the table, ideally near the start (forward) or near the end (backward). And the difference table should settle down to nearly constant at some low order.

When not to use it: If the spacing is unequal, use Lagrange or divided differences (lesson 18). If the data is noisy, a curve that passes through every point also passes through every bit of noise; fit a curve by least squares instead (lesson 20). If you need to extrapolate far outside the table, no polynomial formula is trustworthy, because polynomials shoot off to plus or minus infinity. And if you have many points, a single high-degree polynomial can wiggle badly (lesson 19), so splines are better.

Common mistakes: Using h in the wrong place: p = (x - x0)/h, not x - x0. Using forward differences in the backward formula, or taking differences from the wrong row. Forgetting that p is negative in the backward formula and that the factors are p, p + 1, p + 2 there, not p - 1, p - 2. Dividing by 2 and 6 but forgetting 3! = 6 and 4! = 24 for later terms. A good self-check: plug in p = 0 or p = 1 and confirm you get back a table value exactly.

What exams ask: Build a difference table and estimate a value near the top using the forward formula, and one near the bottom using the backward formula. Derive Newton's forward formula from E = 1 + Δ. Explain why forward is better near the start. Sometimes: find the missing term in a table, assuming a polynomial of given degree (set the right difference to zero and solve).

Mental model: Picture walking along a path with a guide. The forward formula starts at the first lamp post and says: walk p steps at this speed, then adjust for how the speed is changing, then adjust for how that change is changing. Each adjustment is smaller. The backward formula is the same walk, but you start from the last lamp post and walk backward. Pick the lamp post closest to where you want to stand.

Recap: Interpolation estimates values between table points by building a polynomial through them. With equal spacing h, set p = (x - x0)/h and use Newton's forward formula y0 + pΔy0 + p(p - 1)/2! Δ²y0 + ... near the start; use the backward formula with ∇ near the end. Stop adding terms when differences become constant or the terms are tiny. Next, we drop the equal-spacing requirement with Lagrange and divided differences.
key_points: Interpolation builds a polynomial through table points and evaluates it between them; outside the table it is risky extrapolation.
Use p = (x - x0)/h; it counts how many steps x is from the base point.
Forward: f ≈ y0 + pΔy0 + p(p - 1)/2! Δ²y0 + p(p - 1)(p - 2)/3! Δ³y0 + ..., best near the start of the table.
Backward: f ≈ yn + p∇yn + p(p + 1)/2! ∇²yn + ..., with p = (x - xn)/h, best near the end.
Both come from the shift operator: E^p = (1 + Δ)^p or (1 - ∇)^(-p).
Stop adding terms when differences become nearly constant or new terms are smaller than the accuracy you need.
Requires equal spacing and smooth, accurate data.
lessons.tip: After any interpolation, sanity-check by plugging p = 0 and p = 1 into your formula. You must get table values back exactly; if not, a difference or a factorial is wrong.
lessons.task: Use the tea table (0, 90), (10, 75), (20, 64), (30, 56). Estimate the temperature at 15 minutes with the forward formula, then again with the backward formula. Compare the two answers and explain why they agree.

quiz.q: For a table with x0 = 2, h = 0.5, what is p for x = 2.75?
Which formula is best for a value near the end of an equally spaced table?
quiz.explain: The backward formula is built around the last point and backward differences, so it is most accurate near the end.

quiz.q: Table y = x³ at x = 1, 2, 3, 4. Newton's forward formula with three differences gives f(1.5) as:
Why does the term p(p - 1)/2! Δ²y0 not disturb the fit at the first two points?
options: Because p(p - 1) is zero at p = 0 and p = 1
quiz.explain: p(p - 1) vanishes at p = 0 and p = 1, so the correction only affects other points.

quiz.q: Your data is very noisy sensor readings. What is wiser than Newton's interpolation?
options: Fit a smooth curve by least squares
quiz.explain: Interpolation forces the curve through every noisy point; least squares fits the trend instead.

lessons.title: Unequal Spacing: Lagrange and Newton's Divided Differences
lessons.content:
A Pathao rider's phone sends its GPS position to the server, but not at neat, regular times. Sometimes it sends after 2 seconds, sometimes after 3, sometimes after 5, depending on the network. The app still wants to draw the bike smoothly on your map and guess where it was at any moment. Newton's forward and backward formulas from lesson 17 cannot help here, because they need equally spaced x values. This lesson gives two methods that work with any spacing: Lagrange interpolation and Newton's divided differences.

The problem: We have n + 1 points (x0, y0), (x1, y1), ..., (xn, yn) with all x values different, but the gaps between them can be anything. We want the polynomial of degree at most n that passes through all of them, and we want to evaluate it at some new x. Before these methods, people either forced their data onto an equal grid (by re-measuring or by first interpolating linearly) or used only straight lines between neighbours. Both waste accuracy.

One answer only: Here is a key fact. For n + 1 points with distinct x values, there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n through them. Why? Suppose two such polynomials P and Q exist. Their difference P - Q has degree at most n, but it is zero at all n + 1 points. A non-zero polynomial of degree n has at most n roots. So P - Q must be the zero polynomial, meaning P = Q. This matters a lot: Lagrange, Newton forward, Newton backward and divided differences are just different ways of writing the same polynomial. If two methods give different answers on the same points, someone made an arithmetic mistake.

Lagrange's idea, building blocks: Lagrange asked a clever question. Can I build, for each point, a small polynomial that equals 1 at that point and 0 at all the other points? Call it Li(x). If I had those, the answer would simply be P(x) = y0 L0(x) + y1 L1(x) + ... + yn Ln(x). At x = x2, every L is zero except L2, which is 1, so P(x2) = y2. Exactly what we want. It is like a set of switches: at each data point, exactly one switch is on.

Building Li: To make a polynomial zero at every xj except xi, just multiply the factors (x - xj) for all j not equal to i. That product is zero at each of those xj. But at x = xi it is some number, not 1. So divide by the same product evaluated at xi. The result: Li(x) = product over j ≠ i of (x - xj)/(xi - xj). Each Li has degree n, so P has degree at most n.

Worked Lagrange example: Points (0, 1), (1, 3), (3, 13). These come secretly from y = x² + x + 1, so we can check. Find P(2). L0(2) = (2 - 1)(2 - 3) / ((0 - 1)(0 - 3)) = (1)(-1)/3 = -1/3. L1(2) = (2 - 0)(2 - 3) / ((1 - 0)(1 - 3)) = (2)(-1)/(-2) = 1. L2(2) = (2 - 0)(2 - 1) / ((3 - 0)(3 - 1)) = 2/6 = 1/3. So P(2) = 1 × (-1/3) + 3 × 1 + 13 × (1/3) = -1/3 + 3 + 13/3 = 7. And 2² + 2 + 1 = 7. Correct. Notice the Li values add up to 1: -1/3 + 1 + 1/3 = 1. They always do, which is a quick check for your arithmetic.

A second worked example with a story: The rider was at 0 metres at t = 0 s, at 10 m at t = 2 s, and at 40 m at t = 5 s. Where was the bike at t = 3 s? L0(3) = (3 - 2)(3 - 5)/((0 - 2)(0 - 5)) = -2/10 = -0.2. L1(3) = (3 - 0)(3 - 5)/((2 - 0)(2 - 5)) = -6/-6 = 1. L2(3) = (3 - 0)(3 - 2)/((5 - 0)(5 - 2)) = 3/15 = 0.2. Distance = 0 × (-0.2) + 10 × 1 + 40 × 0.2 = 18 metres.

Strengths and weaknesses of Lagrange: The formula is easy to write and easy to understand, and it needs no table. It is great for proofs and small hand problems. But it has two practical weaknesses. First, if you get a new data point, every Li changes, so you start over. Second, evaluating it directly costs about n² multiplications for each new x. There is an improved arrangement called the barycentric form that fixes the cost, but in a first course the usual fix is Newton's divided differences.

Divided differences, the idea: Remember that finite differences measure change per step. When steps are uneven, divide the change by the gap. The first divided difference is f[x0, x1] = (y1 - y0)/(x1 - x0), which is just the slope between two points. The second is f[x0, x1, x2] = (f[x1, x2] - f[x0, x1])/(x2 - x0): how fast the slope changes, divided by the full width. In general, f[x0, ..., xk] = (f[x1, ..., xk] - f[x0, ..., x(k-1)])/(xk - x0). Each new column divides by a wider gap.

Newton's divided difference formula: P(x) = f[x0] + f[x0, x1](x - x0) + f[x0, x1, x2](x - x0)(x - x1) + f[x0, x1, x2, x3](x - x0)(x - x1)(x - x2) + ... It looks just like Newton forward, but with divided differences instead of Δ, and with real distances (x - xi) instead of p. Each term is zero at all earlier points, so adding a term never spoils earlier fits. That is the same clever design as before.

Worked divided difference table: Same points (0, 1), (1, 3), (3, 13). First column: f[0, 1] = (3 - 1)/(1 - 0) = 2, and f[1, 3] = (13 - 3)/(3 - 1) = 5. Second column: f[0, 1, 3] = (5 - 2)/(3 - 0) = 1. So P(x) = 1 + 2(x - 0) + 1(x - 0)(x - 1) = 1 + 2x + x² - x = x² + x + 1. We recovered the hidden formula exactly. P(2) = 7, same as Lagrange, as uniqueness promised.

Adding a point is cheap: Now a new measurement arrives: (4, 21). With Lagrange you rebuild everything. With divided differences you add one row at the bottom: f[3, 4] = (21 - 13)/1 = 8, then f[1, 3, 4] = (8 - 5)/(4 - 1) = 1, then f[0, 1, 3, 4] = (1 - 1)/(4 - 0) = 0. The new term is 0 × (x - 0)(x - 1)(x - 3) = 0. The polynomial stays x² + x + 1, which makes sense because 21 = 4² + 4 + 1. In real use the new coefficient would not be zero, and you just add that one term. The old work is kept.

Useful facts: Divided differences are symmetric: the order of the points does not matter, so f[x0, x1, x2] = f[x2, x0, x1]. For equally spaced points, f[x0, ..., xk] = Δᵏy0 / (k! hᵏ), which shows Newton forward is a special case of divided differences. And if the data comes from a polynomial of degree n, the n-th divided differences are all equal, just like constant n-th differences in lesson 16. Divided differences also approximate derivatives: f[x0, ..., xk] equals f⁽ᵏ⁾(ξ)/k! for some ξ in the range of the points.

Inverse interpolation: Sometimes you know y and want x. For example, which x gives y = 5? If the function is steadily rising or falling in the range, you can just swap the roles of x and y and interpolate x as a function of y with Lagrange. Example: points (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 8) come from y = 2^x. Swap: treat (2, 1), (4, 2), (8, 3) as (y, x). At y = 5, Lagrange gives x = 1 × (5 - 4)(5 - 8)/((2 - 4)(2 - 8)) + 2 × (5 - 2)(5 - 8)/((4 - 2)(4 - 8)) + 3 × (5 - 2)(5 - 4)/((8 - 2)(8 - 4)) = -0.25 + 2.25 + 0.375 = 2.375. The true answer is log2(5), about 2.3219. Close, not perfect, because x as a function of y is a logarithm, not a quadratic. Inverse interpolation is a quick estimate; it is also an idea behind some root-finding methods.

Real-life example 1, map tracking: Ride-sharing and delivery apps receive positions at irregular times. A simple way to draw a smooth path between position reports is to interpolate, separately for latitude and longitude, using time as x. A low-degree interpolation over the last few points can give a neat curve instead of jerky jumps. Real apps also use other filters, but unequal-spacing interpolation is a natural building block.

Real-life example 2, laboratory data: A student in a chemistry lab at Dhaka University measures how much salt dissolves in water at 10, 25, 40 and 70 degrees, because those were the temperatures the water bath reached. The report needs the value at 50 degrees. The temperatures are unequally spaced, so a divided difference table is the right tool. If later she adds a reading at 55 degrees, she just adds a row.

When to use Lagrange: For small hand problems, for proofs, and when you evaluate at only one or two x values and the data will not change. When to use divided differences: When points are unequally spaced and you might add more points, or when you need to evaluate at many x values; you build the table once and evaluate the nested form quickly.

When not to use either: When you have many points (say 15 or more), a single high-degree polynomial often oscillates wildly between points, especially near the ends. Use piecewise methods like splines (lesson 19). When data is noisy, use least squares (lesson 20). And never trust these polynomials far outside the range of x values.

Common mistakes: In Lagrange, students include the j = i factor and divide by zero, or swap numerator and denominator. In divided differences, the most common error is dividing by the neighbouring gap instead of the full width: for f[x0, x1, x2], divide by x2 - x0, not x2 - x1. Another mistake is mixing the order of points between the table and the formula. A quick check: the Lagrange basis values at any x must add to 1, and the final polynomial must reproduce every table value.

What exams ask: Find the Lagrange polynomial through three or four points and evaluate it. Build a divided difference table and write Newton's polynomial. Show that both give the same answer. Prove uniqueness of the interpolating polynomial. Use inverse interpolation to find x for a given y. Show that divided differences are symmetric, or that for equal spacing they reduce to Δᵏy0/(k! hᵏ).

Mental model: Lagrange is a team of spotlights: each spotlight shines fully on its own data point and is dark on all the others; the final curve is the sum of all spotlights, each scaled by its y value. Newton's divided differences is a staircase of corrections: start with a constant, add a slope, then a bend, then a twist, each step chosen so it does not move the points you already fixed.

Recap: For unequally spaced data, the interpolating polynomial is still unique. Lagrange writes it as a sum of yi times basis polynomials Li that are 1 at their own point and 0 elsewhere. Newton's divided differences write it as a growing sum of correction terms, built from a table where each column divides by a wider gap; adding a new point costs only one more row. Both give the same polynomial, so use whichever is easier for the job.
key_points: Through n + 1 points with distinct x values there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n.
Lagrange: P(x) = sum of yi Li(x), where Li(x) = product over j ≠ i of (x - xj)/(xi - xj).
Each Li is 1 at xi and 0 at every other data point; the Li always add up to 1.
Divided differences: f[x0, x1] = (y1 - y0)/(x1 - x0), and each higher order divides by the full width xk - x0.
Newton's form: f[x0] + f[x0, x1](x - x0) + f[x0, x1, x2](x - x0)(x - x1) + ...; adding a point adds one term.
For equal spacing, f[x0, ..., xk] = Δᵏy0/(k! hᵏ).
Inverse interpolation swaps x and y to estimate x for a given y when the function is monotonic.
lessons.tip: Before evaluating a Lagrange polynomial, add up your Li values at that x. If they do not sum to 1, you have an arithmetic slip somewhere, and you can find it before it spoils the final answer.
lessons.task: Take points (1, 1), (2, 4), (4, 16) and estimate the value at x = 3 with both Lagrange and divided differences. You should get 9 both times. Then add the point (5, 25) to your divided difference table and see what the new coefficient is.

quiz.q: Why do Lagrange and Newton's divided difference formula give the same answer on the same points?
options: The interpolating polynomial of degree at most n through n + 1 points is unique
quiz.explain: Two different polynomials of degree at most n cannot agree at n + 1 points, so all methods produce the same polynomial.

quiz.q: What is the main practical advantage of divided differences over Lagrange?
options: They do not need distinct x values
They work only for equal spacing
They give a more accurate polynomial
Adding a new data point only adds one new term
quiz.explain: The polynomial is the same, but Newton's form keeps old work; Lagrange must rebuild every basis polynomial.

quiz.q: In f[x0, x1, x2], what do you divide by?
quiz.explain: A k-th divided difference divides by the full width, the last x minus the first x: here x2 - x0.

quiz.q: What does the Lagrange basis polynomial L1(x) equal at x = x1 and at x = x0?
options: y1 at x1 and y0 at x0
quiz.explain: Each basis polynomial is 1 at its own point and 0 at every other data point.

lessons.title: Interpolation Error and Splines
lessons.content:
Imagine you are drawing a smooth road on a map through ten villages. You try one single curve through all ten. Between the middle villages it looks fine, but near the first and last village the curve swings wildly, as if the road suddenly went for a long detour into a rice field. More points did not make it better; it made it worse. This lesson explains why that happens, how big interpolation errors can be, and the fix engineers use every day: splines, which build the road out of many short, gentle pieces joined smoothly.

The question: In lessons 17 and 18 we built a polynomial P that passes exactly through the data points. At the data points, the error is zero. But between them, P(x) and the true function f(x) can differ. How big can that difference be? And does adding more points always shrink it? Answering these questions honestly is what separates a careful engineer from someone who just presses buttons.

The error formula: If f is smooth enough (it has n + 1 continuous derivatives) and P interpolates f at n + 1 points x0, ..., xn, then for any x in the range, f(x) - P(x) = f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)/(n + 1)! × (x - x0)(x - x1)...(x - xn), where ξ is some unknown point in the interval containing x and all the xi. We do not know ξ exactly, but we can bound the error by using the largest value of |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾| on that interval.

Reading the formula like a story: The error has two parts. The first part, f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾/(n + 1)!, depends on the function: how wiggly it is. If f is itself a polynomial of degree n or less, its (n + 1)-th derivative is zero and the error is zero everywhere, which is why our cube examples were exact. The second part, the product (x - x0)...(x - xn), depends only on where the points are and where x is. It is zero at each data point and grows as x moves away from the points. Far outside the table it becomes huge, which is the mathematical reason extrapolation is dangerous.

Worked error example: Estimate √5 by linear interpolation between √4 = 2 and √9 = 3. The line gives P(5) = 2 + (3 - 2)(5 - 4)/(9 - 4) = 2.2. The true √5 is about 2.2361, so the actual error is about 0.0361. Now the bound: n = 1, so we need the second derivative. For f(x) = √x, f''(x) = -1/(4x^(3/2)). Its largest size on [4, 9] is at x = 4: 1/(4 × 8) = 1/32. The product is |(5 - 4)(5 - 9)| = 4. Bound: (1/32)/2! × 4 = 0.0625. The real error 0.0361 is below the bound 0.0625, as promised. The bound is a guarantee, not a prediction: real errors are often smaller.

A special case worth remembering: For linear interpolation on a single gap of width h, the product (x - x0)(x - x1) is largest in the middle, where it equals h²/4. So the error is at most h²/8 × max|f''|. Halve the gap and the error drops by four. For example, linear interpolation in a table of sin x with step 0.1 has error at most 0.01/8 = 0.00125, because |sin''| is at most 1.

Does more points always help? It is natural to think: more points, higher degree, smaller error. For many nice functions near the middle of the table, that is true. But for equally spaced points it can fail badly. In 1901 Carl Runge studied the innocent-looking function f(x) = 1/(1 + 25x²) on [-1, 1]. It is smooth, bell-shaped, with no jumps. Interpolate it at equally spaced points: with 6 points (degree 5) the largest error on the interval is about 0.43. With 11 points (degree 10), the largest error grows to about 1.9, near x = ±0.94. At x = 0.95, the true value is about 0.042, but the degree 10 polynomial gives about 1.92. Higher degree made it worse. This is called the Runge phenomenon.

Why Runge happens: Look at the error formula again. For equally spaced points, the product (x - x0)...(x - xn) is much larger near the ends of the interval than in the middle. And for Runge's function, the high derivatives grow very fast as n increases. Together, the ends of the interval blow up. The polynomial is forced to hit every point exactly, and to do so with one single formula it must swing up and down between them.

Two cures: The first cure is to choose the points differently. Chebyshev points crowd closer together near the ends of the interval, which keeps the product small everywhere. With Chebyshev points, interpolation of smooth functions like Runge's converges nicely. But often we cannot choose where data comes from; measurements are taken where they are taken. The second cure, much more common in practice, is to stop using one big polynomial and use many small ones. That is piecewise interpolation.

Piecewise linear interpolation: Just connect neighbouring points with straight lines, like a child's join-the-dots drawing. Each piece only uses two points, so nothing can swing wildly. The error on each piece is at most h²/8 × max|f''|, so with small gaps it is accurate. Spreadsheets, graph plotting apps and many lookup tables do exactly this. The weakness: at every data point there is a corner. The slope suddenly changes. For a road, a car's path, a camera's motion in a film, or a font outline, corners look and feel wrong.

Cubic splines, the idea: Use a separate cubic polynomial on each gap, and glue neighbours so that at every inner point the value, the slope (first derivative) and the bending (second derivative) all match. The result looks like one smooth curve, but each piece is only a cubic, so it cannot swing wildly. The name comes from shipbuilding and drafting: a spline was a thin flexible strip of wood, held in place at chosen points by heavy weights. The strip bent smoothly through the points, and mathematically the natural cubic spline behaves much like that strip at small bends.

Counting the unknowns: With n + 1 points there are n gaps, each with a cubic of 4 coefficients, so 4n unknowns. Conditions: each cubic must pass through its two end points: 2n conditions. At each of the n - 1 inner points, slopes match: n - 1 conditions, and second derivatives match: another n - 1. Total 4n - 2. We need two more, chosen at the two ends. A natural spline sets the second derivative to zero at both ends, so the curve straightens out at the edges. A clamped spline uses given slopes at the ends. A not-a-knot spline asks the first two pieces and the last two pieces to be the same cubic.

How it is computed: The neat trick is to use the second derivatives Mi at the points as unknowns. For equal spacing h, matching slopes leads to one simple equation per inner point: M(i-1) + 4Mi + M(i+1) = 6/h² × (y(i-1) - 2yi + y(i+1)). Each equation involves only three neighbouring unknowns, so the system is tridiagonal and can be solved in about n steps instead of n³. That is why splines are cheap even for thousands of points.

Worked natural spline: Points (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0), h = 1. Natural ends: M0 = M2 = 0. The one inner equation: 0 + 4M1 + 0 = 6 × (0 - 2 × 1 + 0) = -12, so M1 = -3. On [0, 1], the spline is S(x) = M1 x³/6 + (y1 - M1 h²/6) x, using the standard formula with M0 = 0 and y0 = 0. That is S(x) = -0.5x³ + 1.5x. At x = 0.5: -0.5 × 0.125 + 0.75 = 0.6875. Check: S(0) = 0, S(1) = -0.5 + 1.5 = 1. Good. By symmetry the piece on [1, 2] mirrors this one. A single quadratic through the same three points, y = 2x - x², gives 0.75 at x = 0.5. The spline is a little flatter, because it straightens out at the ends.

A nice property: Among all smooth functions that pass through the given points, the natural cubic spline has the smallest total squared bending, the integral of (S'')². In plain words, it is the least wiggly curve that still hits every point. That is a strong reason to trust it as a default.

Real-life example 1, design and animation: Car designers, font designers and animators all need smooth curves through chosen points. Design software uses piecewise polynomial curves like splines and Bézier curves, which are close relatives. When an animator in a Dhaka studio sets a character's hand position at a few key frames, the software fills in the in-between frames with a smooth piecewise curve so the hand does not jerk.

Real-life example 2, roads and rails: When engineers plan a new road or railway curve, sudden changes in bending would throw passengers sideways. They join straight sections and curves so that both direction and bending change gradually. The same idea, matching value, slope and curvature at the joins, is what a cubic spline does mathematically.

When to use what: For a few points from a smooth function, a single low-degree polynomial (degree 3 or 4) is fine. For many points, or when you need a smooth curve over a long range, use a cubic spline. For quick lookups where corners do not matter, piecewise linear is enough. If you are free to choose where to sample a function, Chebyshev points make high-degree polynomials safe.

When not to: Do not use high-degree polynomials on many equally spaced points. Do not use interpolation of any kind on noisy data; noise gets traced faithfully and can even be amplified, especially by splines that must bend through each noisy point. Use least squares (lesson 20). And splines, like polynomials, are not good for extrapolation beyond the end points.

Common mistakes: Believing more points always means better accuracy. Forgetting that the error formula needs the (n + 1)-th derivative, not the n-th. Confusing the bound with the actual error. For splines, forgetting the two end conditions, so there are not enough equations, or using M(i-1) + 2Mi + M(i+1) instead of the correct 4 in the middle for equal spacing.

What exams ask: State the interpolation error formula and use it to bound the error of linear or quadratic interpolation. Explain the Runge phenomenon and how to avoid it. Define a cubic spline and list its conditions. Find a natural cubic spline through three or four points and evaluate it.

Mental model: A single high-degree polynomial is like a long stiff rope pinned at many points: to touch every pin it has to whip up and down, worst at the ends. A spline is like a chain of short flexible strips, each one only needs to reach its neighbour, and the joints are smooth, so the whole thing stays calm.

Recap: The interpolation error equals f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)/(n + 1)! times the product of (x - xi); it is zero at the data points, small for smooth functions near the middle, and huge outside the range. For equally spaced points, increasing the degree can make things worse (Runge). Piecewise methods fix this: piecewise linear is simple with corners, and cubic splines are smooth, cheap via a tridiagonal system, and the least wiggly curves through the points.
key_points: Error formula: f(x) - P(x) = f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)/(n + 1)! × (x - x0)(x - x1)...(x - xn).
Error is zero at data points, grows away from them, and is huge in extrapolation.
Linear interpolation on a gap h has error at most h²/8 × max|f''|.
Runge phenomenon: high-degree interpolation at equally spaced points can oscillate wildly near the ends.
Fixes: Chebyshev points if you can choose them, or piecewise methods.
A cubic spline uses one cubic per gap, matching value, slope and second derivative at inner points.
Natural spline: second derivative zero at both ends; the system is tridiagonal and cheap.
The natural cubic spline is the least wiggly (smallest integral of (S'')²) curve through the points.
lessons.tip: Whenever you interpolate, plot or sketch the result between points, not just at them. Runge-type wiggles and spline overshoots are obvious to the eye and invisible in a table of values at the data points.
lessons.task: Find a natural cubic spline through (0, 0), (1, 2), (2, 0) by hand: write the one equation for M1, solve it, and evaluate the spline at x = 0.5. Then compare with the quadratic through the same three points.

quiz.q: For data from a polynomial of degree 2, what is the error of quadratic interpolation through 3 points?
options: Zero only at the data points
quiz.explain: The third derivative of a degree 2 polynomial is zero, so the error formula gives zero everywhere.

quiz.q: What is the Runge phenomenon?
options: Splines failing at their end points
Wild oscillation near the ends when interpolating many equally spaced points with one high-degree polynomial
quiz.explain: Runge showed that for 1/(1 + 25x²), increasing degree at equally spaced points makes the error near the ends grow.

quiz.q: Linear interpolation of sin x with step h = 0.1 has error at most about:
Which conditions does a cubic spline enforce at every inner point?
options: Equal values, slopes and second derivatives
quiz.explain: A cubic spline matches value, first derivative and second derivative at every inner point.

quiz.q: What does a natural cubic spline assume at the two ends?
quiz.explain: Natural end conditions set S'' = 0 at both ends, so the curve straightens out there.

lessons.title: Curve Fitting by Least Squares
lessons.content:
